Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present a petition signed by several persons from Nova Scotia.
They call upon the government to cease with its proposed shift of the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of through a real tax reform.
In other words, they call upon the government to withdraw the GST legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table two petitions that add to the former petitions dealing with the imposition of the new sales tax on reading.
These petitioners take strong exception to the government's intentions to impose a GST on books. They state clearly that since Confederation no government has dared do this. This government is certainly to be condemned for its measures.
The petitioners say that the uninhibited dissemination of the printed word as a corner-stone of democracy, culture, education and a literate and productive society will be negatively affected by the GST applications.
The undersigned pray and call upon Parliament to re-affirm the historic principles embodied in the free status of all taxes for the printed word by retaining the zero rate applied for years to books and publications.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition duly certified from members of my constituency in Punnichy, Saskatchewan.
They call upon the government and Parliament to reject the current proposal for a goods and services tax, to reform the taxation system so there is an effective minimum tax on wealthy individuals and corporations, in short, to engage in real tax reform instead of the regressive reforms proposed by this government.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I wish to table a petition from residents of Senneterre, in Abitibi, who call upon the Government of Canada to scrap the so-called Hill project, which, at a cost of $68 million, would provide for the construction of an underground parking garage and shopping mall under the Parliament Buildings. Your petitioners recognize the need to preserve the environment and historic character of the Parliament Buildings and Parliament Hill in Ottawa.
Your petitioners also maintain that members should continue to park in the spaces behind the Parliament Buildings, and park outside like our factory workers in this country, and that the Government of Canada has better things to do than to provide an underground parking garage and shopping mall on the Hill for members of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to file a petition with the House, under Standing Order 36, from the people of Port Alberni, British Columbia.
The petitioners say that they are fed up with the service cutbacks at Canada Post and fed up with management and direction by government that places customer service at the bottom of the priority list. In particular, they request of Parliament that Canada Post reopen the drive-through postal drop-off service at Port Alberni, and also that Canada Post Corporation be instructed to keep existing outlets open, to operate longer hours, to expand revenue generating services, to stop privatizing,

Government Orders
and to start increasing services in order to retain revenues.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from the residents of Coquitlam, Port Coquitlam, and Port Moody, British Columbia in my riding. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have been fighting a battle to get cable companies regulated.
These petitioners say that cable companies are making an average 32 per cent profit on fixed assets, whereas phone companies are making half that. The petitions humbly pray and call upon Parliament to adopt Bill C-284, which is my private members' bill, to apply rate of return regulations so that the cable industry will be regulated like the phone industry and Canadians will have lower cable rates.

The House resumed from Thursday, November 1, consider of Bill C-40, an act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and Motions Nos. 12 to 15 of Mrs. Finestone (p. 14979); and Motion No. 42 of Mr. Edwards (p. 14979).

Mr. Speaker, as you have just indicated, we are resuming debate on motions which include the excellent motions of the hon. member for Mount Royal which are before us for discussion. The motions presented by the hon. member for Mount Royal reflect, in essence, the deep dissatisfaction with the substance of Bill C-40. We have to register such a feeling in the context of report stage.
The dissatisfaction flows from the key issue of the removal from the 1968 mandate given to the CBC to contribute to the development of national unity and to provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity.
The removal of a national unity reference in the CBC mandate was recommended by two initiatives. One was the Caplan-Sauvageau report in 1986 and the other

Government Orders
subsequently came from the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture the year after. Both were concerned that this particular mandate of contributing to the development of national unity might, and I quote from their report, "interfere with the CBC's ability to ensure that its programming reflects and interprets as fully and fairly and accurately as possible Canada's cultural, social, political, economic, linguistic and regional reality and diversity".
I submit that this is rubbish. It is unadulterated nonsense. It is an abandonment and almost a betrayal of the original purpose and mandate that appropriately was given to the CBC in 1968 when its linguistic, cultural and social role was given a modern interpretation and a badly needed one.
A former president of the CBC, Pierre Juneau, when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Communications said that the phrase "national unity" had not caused any problems during his years as president of the CBC. It is worth noting that the CRTC noted that its interpretation of the term never precluded a free political discussion from all points of view.
In that context, we are very distressed to see that the Minister of Communications, who is in the House today, also drank the same bathtub water produced by the Caplan-Sauvageau report and subscribed to that rubbish as well. I am very disappointed because I always thought that, in philosophical and political terms, he was very much in favour of developing and maintaining strong bonds across Canada.
It is not just the fact that the CBC's appropriation was cut by $240 million over the last six years by the government that is creating unhappiness on this side of the House. The motions before us surround this dissatisfaction. It is the dropping of the national mandate given to the CBC. There is no amount of outrage that can reflect sufficiently the profound distaste for this measure contained in the bill proposed by the Conservative government. However, it comes as no surprise, considering the composition of the caucus and the recent transfers across the floor of the House from the government caucus to the independent benches.
Evidently, their interpretation of national unity is a very shaky one. It is a very shaky political alliance anyway, and it has given in recent time indications of falling apart.
We believe, as it was very well put in The Ottawa Citizen in May of this year, that the CBC is an agent for Canadian unity and that it must remain that way, that it is a bulwark against various decentralizing forces. It was in September of this year put very well in the Globe and Mail by Steven Godfrey who, among others, wrote on the CBC that Parliament should reject this bill as the cynical piece of work it is, making specific reference to the question of the dropping of the national unity clause. It seems as though the government has abandoned the basic principles that have determined the action and the spirit of this very important institution.
I would like to put on record some of the principles as restated in recent weeks by the Friends of the CBC movement, which is a coalition of artists, writers and the like, and who have somehow pledged their commitment to the CBC in the following terms. First, they see Canada as a place for a lively broadcasting industry which should have a strong and healthy balance between the public and the private stations. They believe that the CBC, both radio and television, is the most important element of the Canadian broadcasting system, and so do we. They believe that the CBC must continue to be a public service broadcaster and a dynamic alternative to the commercial networks and stations. They oppose the introduction of advertising on CBC radio and stereo, and the recent trends of increasing publicity and commercialization on the CBC television network.
In addition, they believe that the CBC must provide a balanced program service, a service which informs, enlightens, entertains, and meets the particular needs of a variety of specialized audiences. They believe that CBC programming should reflect and serve all parts of the country. They support a level of funding for the CBC that permits it to carry out its statutory mandate and here, of course, we come to the question of cuts and, therefore, a requirement to increase its funding. It is, with regret, that we know that our network in Canada is lagging behind other national networks, particularly the European ones, where there is a network one, a network two, and a network three, which try to meet the needs of different audiences.

Finally, the Friends of the CBC support an increased Canadianization of the airwaves. This eight-point set of principles was produced and distributed by a well-known Canadian author and writer, Peter Newman.
At this stage, of course, it is late to reorganize and to modify appropriately Bill C-40. Nevertheless, it is important to put on record these views because this bill, if passed, will hopefully be proclaimed, implemented and enforced only for a short time, that is, between now and the next election. At the time of the next election, I am sure that an electorate, enraged for a variety of reasons to which Bill C-40 has to be added, will take care of the wrong directions in which the government is leading Canada. Then we will see to it that the CBC is restored to its original mandate.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to this Bill C-40, an act respecting broadcasting, especially at a time when major decisions are going to be made, within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that will drastically affect not only the quality of our programming but the variety of services that we have been proud of for so long. I refer, specifically, to Radio-Canada International. RCI has been in existence since 1942 and, although some changes have been made to the service, the principle remains the same. That is, and I quote: "to convey objective information and balanced comment, thus reflecting the fullest possible freedom of expression".
Motion No. 15, the motion of our Liberal critic, the member for Mount Royal, and Motion No. 42, the government motion, contained, if you will, the future of an effective service.
If the information regarding CBC's projected $100 million budgetary shortfall is correct, there is nothing in this act to protect Radio Canada International from being eliminated altogether. Under Bill C-40, CBC is not required to operate an international service. It may do so if it so desires.
Motion No. 15 would prevent that, and I would like to share it with the members in the House:
Motion No. 15
That Bill C-40 be amended in Clause 3 by adding immediately
after line 20 at page 5 the following:
Government Orders
(m) the Corporation should provide an international service subject to such applicable statutes and regulations as the Governor in Council may deem necessary;
Since you, Mr. Speaker, have grouped Motions Nos. 15 and 42 for debate, I would like to make a few comments about the government motion.
The government motion says:
(2) The Corporation shall, within the conditions of any licence or licences issued to it by the Commission and subject to any applicable regulations of the Commission, provide an international service in accordance with such directions as the Governor in Council may issue.
It is not very often that I praise the government, but in this case, I do praise the government because its motion is even stronger. It said:
(2) The Corporation shall-provide an international service
Whereas the Liberal resolution says:
(m) the Corporation should
I think we should all support Motion No. 42 where it says:
(2) The Corporation shall,
In other words, it must provide such a service.
Mr. Speaker, before I forget, I do want to mention that I do not like the words at the end of the government motion which say:
-with such directions as the Governor in Council may issue.
I will bring in an amendment to that motion at the end of my debate.
Usually, when programs have to be cut or reduced, they are phased out over a period of time. RCI does not even have that protection. To protect our international image, if reductions have to be made, I hope RCI will play an integral role in the decisions, and that any decision will be allowed a period of three to five years to take effect.
Hopefully, we will not even need that period.
My other concern has to do with the risk inherent in RCI being funded from the cultural envelope. The priority for the cultural envelope is servicing Canadians.
The priority for Radio Canada International is to reflect the spectrum of Canadian life and opinion to an international audience, although RCI does provide some programming for Canadians abroad.

November 27, 1990
Government Orders
I would suggest that the funding for RCI be left to those who understand what best serves Canada's national interest. I would not, however, go as far as suggesting that the Department of External Affairs manage the service, because it is the very independence of the service from the government that gives it the unique characteristics to make it as credible as the BBC.
I was impressed in the sixties when we had student exchanges with an American college, Alliance College in Pennsylvania. The president of Alliance College told us that he listened to nothing but CBC, Radio Canada.
I felt very good as a Canadian. Here is a president of an American college not listening to any American programs, but listening to our CBC.
I would suggest, however, that the responsibility for funding be moved to the external affairs and international trade envelope. This argument is especially important today. We are spending literally millions of dollars on trade delegations all over the world to make international markets more aware of Canadian trade opportunities, and millions on supporting trade with the Soviet Union and eastern Europe as encouragement in their struggle for democracy.
Yet, we are actually considering taking away one of the more effective and inexpensive means to reach and achieve exactly those goals.
I have on numerous occasions expressed concern about the government's commitment to following through with programs that it established. Just over three weeks ago, we debated the new and expanded role of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. We talked about the need to exchange technologies, information and the importance of discussing long and openly, if need be, to reach consensus among all countries involved.
We are still awaiting the return of Bill C-88, a bill that deals with Canada's contribution to the European Bank for reconstruction and development. Once again, they are the same concerns about the political will to follow through.
I do not think you would find too many objections to any of these initiatives if there was confidence in the motives for all these initiatives. But we keep seeing the
introduction of new ones, while others lay by the wayside, forgotten.
One way to show that the government is serious about all these endeavours is to commit directly to keeping Radio Canada International alive so that the people in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe know about our desire and our efforts to see them through these difficult times.
I broke away from a three-day conference held here in Ottawa. The name of the conference is "The Changing Soviet Union: Implications for Canada and the World". I was impressed how the organizers found funding in a very creative way. They did not have enough money in one envelope from one department, so they found money from National Defence Canada, Industry, Science and Technology Canada, Indian and Northern Affairs Canada, External Affairs and International Trade, the Disarmament Fund, Parliamentary Centre for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, and the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. So there are creative waves of coming up with funding. Maybe it is time that RCI be funded from the external affairs envelope, rather than the cultural envelope.
I cannot emphasize the importance of the free and independent Canadian international service. I stress "Canadian" because -although the way this government is going, I am not sure how long this will last-we may find that to tune in to Canadian opinion, one need only turn on Voice of America. Hopefully this will never happen again because to date there is still great affection and respect for a news service that is Canadian. It is still felt that a Canadian news service is impartial and by being impartial it is encouraging to those populations in countries where censorship and news are synonymous.
One of the more recent examples that typifies this particular situation is the events that took place in Tiananmen Square. We were able to reach the students and convey to them our reaction to the tragic events. We were able to let them know that Canada was not going to send Chinese students back to China, that we were going to offer them refuge.
You are giving me the signal, Mr. Speaker, that the time is up. I have a lot more to debate here, but I do want to table an amendment to Motion No. 42 which would read:

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to participate in this very important debate at report stage of this very important Bill C-40.
Government Orders
I want to keep my comments to a number of the proposed amendments, the motions before us in the grouping. There are five motions in this grouping, three of which I want to speak to in particular.
At the outset I should say that I support each of the amendments in this grouping.
The first one, Motion No. 12, deals very specifically with the parliamentary service. In a modem democracy, especially when we look at what is happening around the world, countries such as Yugoslavia, which I visited recently with some other parliamentarians, are experiencing for the first time a multi-party democratic election. We see that all over eastern Europe. Countries have to work as best they can to deliver the institutions to the people. What I mean is that in a place like Canada, this body here which is the highest court in the land, the Parliament of Canada, must take every means possible and use everything at her disposal to ensure that the people of Canada have access to their parliamentarians and can watch Parliament in action.
One way that that can be done, very clearly, is through the parliamentary channel. The parliamentary channel has been a great experiment in Canadian politics. I think now we have over 440,000 households on average watching Question Period every day of the week that this place sits. That is important because in a modem democratic state, televised proceedings of the legislature of the Parliament is a check on abuse by governments. It means that the people of Canada can watch their parliamentarians in action and when governments choose to abuse or override the rales or have the tyranny of the majority- which happens many times in this place-the people of Canada can tune in on their television, unobstructed, without editorial comment, without filtering by a news agency, and watch Parliament in action. That is very important.
The motion that we have before us, Motion No. 12, is very important because it would mandate CBC under this legislation to provide a parliamentary service. I know there is a committee of the House that is looking at better ways to deliver the proceedings of this place and of the committees of this place via the air waves. At some point it will make a report and the report will be debated. But I would hope that we understand that the CBC has a mandate and it is a mandate of national unity. Part of its new mandate, I believe, is to ensure that

November 27, 1990
Government Orders
never, ever, will commercial considerations or time considerations between conflicting priorities of the cable company overtake the ability of the Canadian public to watch Parliament in action. The CBC is such a body. The CBC is the vehicle that should be mandated specifically by statute to ensure that Canadians everywhere have a right of access through their televisions to what happens in this Parliament.
We know that many times a government, not just this government but more particularly this government, would like to ensure that the record of the House is not properly distributed to everybody in the country because sometimes governments make mistakes.
Especially this government.

Especially this government. It is notorious for it. A parliamentary channel mandated through a vehicle of national unity like the CBC is the way to ensure the independence and access of every Canadian to the proceedings of the highest court in the land, the Parliament of Canada.
I would like to address Motion 14 because it really concerns me. This motion is one that I really hope all members in this House will support. It is an important motion. I come from Atlantic Canada. Unfortunately or fortunately, we have had to grow up watching the reporting of what goes on in this great nation from a central Canadian bias. The CBC, Global, and CTV obviously have to play to the ratings. They have to pay the bills at the end of the month. Those news organizations have mastered and got into the five-second or the ten-second clip, the sound bite, for the evening news because they only have a fifteen-minute or half-hour newscast.
What happens perhaps in Cape Breton Island or Newfoundland or Fogo Island may not be of such national importance in the view of the editors of those newscasts that it is going to show up on a national news report that evening. I do not fault them for that. That is the reality of the modem world. They have to pay their bills. If they are broadcasting news that does not appeal to the millions of people who live in this unbalanced country, because too many people live at the centre and too few outside the centre, they are not going to get their rates for their advertising and therefore they are not going to be competitive.
All of a sudden what appeared on the scene was CBC Newsworld in English. CBC Newsworld in my view-and I have said this to the director out of the Halifax operation-has provided a tool for national unity and understanding in this country. CBC Newsworld does not have to master the 15, the 10 or the 5 second clip for a 30-minute newscast. The mandate of CBC Newsworld is to report the news from around the world but, more particularly, from around this country.
I have learned more about Alberta from watching CBC Newsworld than from reading any newspaper in this country or any combination of newspapers. I have learned more about the problems of the farmers in Saskatchewan by watching CBC Newsworld because its mandate is different. Its mandate is to try to give a balanced view of news from across the country; not a biased view focused toward the centre, which is Ontario and Quebec, where most of the people live. It has done something different.
It started out as perhaps a Canadian version CNN, that great American all-news network that gives us a great American slant on every piece of world news, national news, or local news that it puts out. However, it has developed into something much more than that. It has developed into a piece of national infrastructure that promotes national unity and understanding in this country. I do not think anybody in this country or on any side of this House who has watched that service would disagree withjne. It has been a refreshing break from the divisiveness and the isolationism that are all too often practised by Canadians in their regions and in their local areas. It is something that absolutely must be protected.
Motion No. 14. which says that there should be a French CBC all-news network is something which is very important. Nobody in this House has to be reminded of the difficulties we have between English Canada and French Canada. They are real and they are severe. Any vehicle that can appeal or deliver itself to the masses, which will increase the level of understanding between English Canadians and French Canadians, should be something that we should support whole-heartedly. We should find the money, no matter where we have to scrape it up, because it is an instrument of national unity.
This motion makes sure that at some future point, because of economic considerations, CBC Newsworld does not have to go out of business. This motion makes sure that CBC Newsworld does not have to alter its
November 27, 1990

format because of commercial considerations, because it has to make a profit. This motion ensures that CBC Newsworld and the benefit that we get in English Canada where it is shown of understanding the diversity and the richness of this country in its cultural, ethnic and regional diversity, are also available to people of the French language who live in Quebec and in other parts of Canada. Examples are the Acadians in Atlantic Canada and the French in the west.
I would hope that this motion in particular be really seriously considered by members opposite. I know that all too often in this House we vote strictly along party lines. If there is an amendment to the government bill, government members opposite think: My God, the House is going to come down on top of us if we agree that an opposition motion makes the legislation better. This is one of those cases where it not only would make the legislation better, but it would make the nation a more tolerant, hospitable and unified country in which to live.
In closing, I would just like to say that these motions that were put forward by my colleague from Mount Royal are thoughtful motions. They have been put forward in the spirit of keeping a national institution a national institution, and that is the CBC. Instead of shrinking its mandate to expand it by statute to ensure that when budget considerations come, as they currently are right now with massive cuts at CBC, some of the important aspects of Canadian unity and Canadian unity infrastructure such as the CBC are not tampered with by a budget axe but are mandated by the Parliament of Canada.
I would hope that members on all sides of the House would see fit to support these motions.

Mr. Speaker, I have already spoken on this group of amendments, but the Liberal Party member has seen fit to amend one of the amendments, so therefore I am entitled to speak again. It is very interesting what has happened here, because the amendment was originally a government amendment, subamended by the Liberal Party. The government amendment states:
Government Orders
The Corporation shall, within the conditions of any licence or licences issued to it by the Commission and subject to any applicable regulations of the Commission, provide an international service in accordance with such directions as the Governor in Council may issue.
What the government has put in the bill is to guarantee really an international service. We have just heard this week that the government proposes to cut Radio Canada International. I say to the minister that he cannot put that in the bill and at the same time turn around and eliminate Radio Canada International.
Why does the government want to cut Radio Canada International? It is part of a pattern to cut back and to threaten not only the independence but the very existence of the CBC. We have seen throughout the Mulro-ney government's mandate the systematic attack on the budget of the CBC. I have said it has leeched the CBC. It has also meeched it too, but we will come back to that when we debate the national unity clause.
The CBC has cut back its regional programming. It has been forced to behave like every other private broadcaster with an eye to the bottom line. The CBC has been stripped of its ability to do good regional programming. Now it will be stripped of its ability to do international programming. We will get a CBC, at least for English television, that is concentrated in Toronto. All the money will be in the Peter and Wendy and Barbara show and so on. I suggest that members might want to read Rick Salutin article in Saturday Night magazine. It is a devastating criticism of what is happening to the CBC.
I want to focus on something else when I see the minister here. I want to focus on real dollars. What I have done is have had a look at what has happened to the CBC's finances, and I just want to go over that. I am talking about allocations in 1988 dollars. I am going to give some figures for appropriations for operations and for commercial revenues, because my submission is that the CBC is becoming more and more commercial, becoming more and more like any other network. Therefore, when we see the CBC logo on television, it just becomes like any other station, and it is not distinctively Canadian.
The CBC, for example, has been forced to abandon its goal of having 95 per cent Canadian content in prime time. It has been forced, as I have already said, to

Government Orders
abandon its goal of having regional programming, which has been cut back 30 per cent.
I remember that years ago the CBC used to reflect Canadians to Canadians all across the country. Ten or fifteen years ago, we could see on prime time television The Plouffe Family, a family in Quebec. It was reflected to those of us who live in western Canada. We could see western Canadian programs that were reflected to other aspects of the country. We could see Don Messer's Jubliee from the Maritimes, which took some of that culture and reflected it across the country. There were four, five or six prime time shows from different regions in Canada that reflected the regions to Canadians. Now we do not have anything like that, and I will tell the House why.
In 1984 to 1985, the appropriations budget-and I am doing this in 1988 dollars-was $943.3 million and the capital budget was $93 million, for a total of about $1 billion. The commercial revenues were $265 million. That was 20 per cent of the budget. In 1985 to 1986, the appropriations operations go down to $879 million and commercial revenues go up to $268 million, some 22 per cent. In 1986 to 1987, $849 million for operations and revenues of 23 per cent. In 1987 to 1988, $828 million with revenues of 26 per cent. In 1988 to 1989, $814 million with revenues of 28 per cent. In 1989 to 1990, $812 million and commercial revenues of $374 million. Almost 30 per cent of the CBC budget is now in commercial revenues.
The minister over there just put everyone in a panic when he came before the committee and said: "Maybe we should get rid of ads". If we got rid of ads, the CBC could not even operate at all. Now the government has backtracked. The Toronto Star has quoted a policy proposal that in fact advertising come to CBC Radio. I like CBC Radio. I like listening to the Gzowski Show and the other shows. I like the fact that it is not beholden to commercial revenue. Leave that for the private sector and keep the CBC unique. This government is meeching and leeching the CBC. The radio network has been especially hurt.
The CRTC said in its most recent licence renewal that the CBC could not fulfil its mandate at current funding levels. Since then funding levels have declined further. In response to the questions before the standing committee on broadcasting last May, CBC Vice-President
Michael McEwan said: "You are right. We are getting squeezed and each year. We have to factor in how we are doing to do that. This year, 1989-90, they lost a 1 per cent real cut across the radio system". They managed to sustain their activity for one more year. As the president, Mr. Veilleux, said: "If we keep going, something is going to have to give, and then you start talking about making decisions. Do you change the nature of how you express all your services? Do you lose some service? Do you lop off an arm rather than deleting the whole thing? These are the issues we are going to have to deal with if we keep heading down this road".
The government is sending contradictory signals. In its broadcasting policy Canadian Voices, Canadian Choices, the government said: "To capture an audience share consistent with the size of its parliamentary appropriation and to be able to generate sufficient commercial revenues, the CBC needs to reach large audiences". Yet, at the legislative committee, the minister emphasized CBC's cultural role and, as I said, he caused a near panic by suggesting that the commission might give up its commercial revenue.
The government has got to get a consistent policy. It has brought in an amendment to the bill to say that it is going to institutionalize Radio Canada International. Then it announced a couple of weeks later that it was thinking of cutting Radio Canada International.
It says it wants a national system; then it cuts regional programs. The minister says: "Maybe we should cut commercials". On the other hand 30 per cent of the CBC budget, as I have shown by figures, is in fact through commercial appropriations. This government has no consistent policy. I am glad the minister is in the House today, but it is about time that he paid some attention to what is going on in communications. I call him Oscar Masse, accepting Oscars in Hollywood or jetting off to Rome.
I am glad the minister is here so he can deal with the real question of communications policy. The role of the CBC in international, national and regional programming is absolutely vital in this country. This is part of the glue that keeps Canada together.
That is why we, in the NDP, have proposed amendments with respect to national unity, the make-up of the
November 27, 1990

CBC, keeping the CBC independent, getting it well funded and putting it in the right direction.
In the next year, we are facing a constitutional crisis in this country. We are going to need a strong CBC that reflects fairly the major issues in this country. We are going to need to reflect Canada to the world. That is why I am glad the government has brought in this amendment.
I say to the minister that he should not be inconsistent. Do not bring in this amendment and then turn around and cut all the funds in the CBC, especially the funds for the international service.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate, and I am delighted to see the minister in our midst. Some words of welcome are in order, and it is a great pleasure to see him back in the House. I must say we missed him, and it is indeed a pleasure to see him here today.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the minister has had time to read the amendments with the requisite care, especially those put forward by our colleague, the hon. member for Mount Royal. The hon. member put a great deal of time and effort into these amendments and came up with some excellent ones which I will now mention, if I may, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for Mount Royal wants the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to provide an all-news service in French and English, a service that is badly needed. There is, of course, Newsworld on the English network, which I think is very good and which provides a 24-hour service. However, although this is excellent for Canadians, at the present time we do not have a similar service in French, although the need is there.
Mr. Speaker, during the crisis at Oka last summer, for instance, we could get a steady stream of information on the English channel, while no similar service was available in French. I think Canadians, whether they are French-speaking or English-speaking, had the right to be informed about a matter of this importance, whatever their position happened to be on this question.
The fact remains that we had the right, as I see it, to be better informed on this question, and when I say we, I
Government Orders
mean the French-speaking population. In fact, we were not getting the same level of service in French as we were getting in English because of the lack of a 24-hour tv news channel.
Mr. Speaker, I am one of the members in this House who had the privilege of learning both official languages of our country at a very early age, and I regularly watch the news on television in French and in English. I often wonder whether several times a week, we could perhaps translate the French news on Radio-Canada into English and take the English news on the CBC and translate it into French, so that Canadians would know what is happening on the other network, because the news we get on the English network is often quite different from the news we get on the French network, reflecting a different perspective.
As far as the regional question is concerned, I think the French network concentrates far too much on central Canada and tells us very little about remote areas, unlike the English network which does a better job.
I think it would be an interesting exercise to let French-speaking Canadians see the English news, translated into French of course, and vice versa, as I said earlier. I think Canadians need more exposure to the news broadcast in the other official language.

Mr. Speaker, I think we should also compliment the hon. member for Mount Royal for proposing to this House that there should be an inclusion in the bill regarding northern service and, of course, regarding Radio Canada International. When we speak about the northern service, again we are talking about an amendment that was proposed by our colleague from Mount Royal who, very thoughtfully, proposed that there be such a reference in the bill. I say to the minister, across the way, that he should stop being so partisan and look at things objectively.
He is not listening.
