speechtext:
I know the minister is listening; he is listening attentively, I can tell. With the close attention that he is paying to this debate, I am sure that he will want to consider the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Mount Royal. I see him nodding, right now, in favour of those amendments. I am sure that that nod

November 27, 1990
Government Orders
indicates that the minister wants to approve those amendments of the member for Mount Royal.
Now in the unlikely event that he is so biased that he refuses to consider those amendments, I will say that it is to the peril of this government. More importantly, I think we must entrench in legislation the need to have the CBC and Radio Canada not only transmit programming to Canadians but transmit information to Canadians which will assist the theme of national unity.
I know that will be addressed in a later amendment but I still wanted to take this very brief opportunity to raise it now because the need to promote national unity is an important component in the job of the CBC and Radio-Canada. I think it should be part of their mandate. I intend to support the amendments of my colleague, the hon. member for Mount Royal, to that effect and to support her tremendous initiatives in improving this bill.
In conclusion, we must not only continue to ensure that the CBC operates well and in the interests of Canada, we cannot take chances with the government across the way, and we must include in legislation some of the components of the CBC mandate to ensure that in a fit of privatization or cutting back, such as the Tories take from time to time, the government does not sacrifice some very valuable programming of the CBC.
I want to make one further point which relates to the parliamentary service. Again, that is set out in Motion No. 12, proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Mount Royal. I know that the parliamentary service is available to a large number of Canadians at the present time, but access to the parliamentary service should be made even easier. I say this because a number of cable distributors have made it such that the parliamentary service is only accessible by means of a television converter. I cannot see why it cannot be one of the basic channels for at least one parliamentary service.
I would even go further and say that all three channels should be on the converter so that Canadians can listen to the House of Commons in the language spoken from the floor, as well as in their choice of English or French, but all three could be on cable and at least one of them should be available on the basic service without the converter.
I conclude with those comments and I ask the minister, across the way, to support the amendments of the hon. member for Mount Royal.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by following up on the comments of my colleague who raised a very good point about availability of the CBC Parliamentary channel on the regular service. Several cable companies have put it into a channel which cannot be reached by low-income Canadians.
I know in my riding where people have an older TV and cannot afford to buy a new TV they cannot watch the proceedings of the House of Commons when they are carried on a channel in the 20's. This coverage is one way we have of communicating with Canadians.
There are a whole range of problems. I wish the government, through the CRTC, would show more concern about this removal of service. It is not a small issue for Canadians, just one of those issues that gets lost in the shuffle. There are many low-income Canadians who wish the opportunity to participate in these debates through watching them and writing letters to the members when they agree or disagree with us. That simply is not available if it requires a new TV or a converter.
I would like to talk in this debate about the role of CBC in these particular areas. When I was listening to the debate a few days ago, I was struck by the number of members from all parties who stood up in support of the CBC and recognized that this government was not showing to Canadians the support that it has traditionally shown to the Crown corporation.
Throughout the last 50 years of broadcasting in Canada, the CBC has been a cornerstone of how we communicate. It has become a greater preoccupation as we enter into the debate on national unity. Every day the newspapers have one story after another about the near collapse of the country, the depression that we feel, our inability to communicate with each other. We realize that for any party to put this country back together, it must find the building blocks. The CBC, now as in the past, is one of those building blocks.
I know there has been a great deal of criticism, as alluded to by another member, and that journalists had been attacking the CBC, but that is part of the game. There are times when the CBC does a good job. There
November 27, 1990

are other times, like any other Crown corporation, when it does not do such a good job. Nevertheless, taking an historical perspective, CBC is one of the few building blocks that we have for communicating among Canadians.
In order to begin to set out a national dream and find a sense of purpose for Canadians, we need a vehicle by which to to communicate. The drive behind that communication cannot simply be commercial interest. There also has to be a non-profit, public purpose organization which can drive us into a forum which allows us to communicate through the regular broadcast of news services and the specials that can be put on in the public affairs area give CBC a role to perform.
Perhaps one of the most important services that is provided to us is the CBC English and French radio services which provide a commonalty of communications through all the remote areas. It does not matter whether you live in Toronto, like my colleague, in my riding in Winnipeg, or in the Northwest Territories as other colleagues do, there is a commonalty there.
If you accept that CBC is one of the building blocks that we should be protecting and enhancing, we have to make sure that the CBC services which are of value to the country are protected. For example, the parliamentary service, which I already discussed, is considered to be a key window for Canadians to view Parliament. Canadians deserve access to its proceedings.
The challenge for us as parliamentarians is to ensure that the new legislative framework and funding arrangements will make adequate and appropriate provision for the full and effective use of the parliamentary channel. I think there can be a great deal of expansion if it is properly funded. That should not be left silent in the legislation. There should be an amendment to show our support for the parliamentary service.
In light of what is happening in the Middle East right now, one of the most important services is Radio Canada International. Our critic, the member for Mount Royal, yesterday asked the government if it was still supportive of Radio Canada International particularly in the Arabic services in the Middle East.
Government Orders
When you see how quickly propaganda can be used to put us on the edge of war, a peaceful way of communicating to a captive audience-captive in someone else's hands rights now-is very important. Again we just cannot assume that the corporation will protect those in times of cutbacks. We have to say through Parliament that this is one of the services that we want it to protect and we are willing to pay for it.
Third, there is the all-news service. One of the great experiments in Canada in the last year has been the development of Newsworld. I can attest as a parliamentarian just how dramatically it has changed the coverage of Parliament and the coverage of other events.
Canadians now participate much more closely with world events because they are brought to us in an immediate fashion. It does not matter whether we are talking about the justice inquiry into aboriginal affairs in Manitoba or the inquiry into abuse in Newfoundland. No issue is too small and no issue is too big to be shared by Canadians.
What Newsworld does in terms of communications is that it pulls away the cost factor of big-time television and, more important, it removes the time factor to allow for the greater explanation of events and permit people to see things unfold, rather than be compacted into a 15-second clip, or compacted into a 90-second item. The subject can be expanded so that people who are really interested in an issue have an opportunity to see it take place.
For example, on Newsworld out of Winnipeg there is a call-in program on which Canadians have an opportunity at noon each day of the week, except for weekends, to phone in and to speak about issues of the day.
We as parliamentarians get a little lazy, I think, because we accept that we have an opportunity to stand up in the House whenever we want to express our opinions. For every one of us there are 80,000 Canadians who do not have that opportunity and it is our responsibility to give them every avenue possible so their views can be expressed. They have a way of talking about the problems facing this country without going through politicians. They should be able to do so just by picking up the phone and talking to people, or watching television to see somebody talking about Parliament, again not

Government Orders
in a 90-second clip, but at great length and in great detail.
These are the sorts of services which are needed. In a country becoming as impoverished as Canada is becoming, mainly because of the laziness of the government in taxation issues, and its inability to manage the economy and where we are faced with such an overwhelming debt, people begin to feel that they cannot afford to do this or cannot afford to do that. They feel that maybe television and radio are not important. It is time to stand up right now and say that these services are important and that the purpose of Parliament is to protect those services from people who do not understand their importance.
Obviously, in this debate the government does not understand the importance of the CBC. Perhaps it is because the Liberal Party is so proud of its tradition of building national organizations, of supporting national institutions, that we naturally rise up to the occasion to defend the CBC. We are astonished by the silence in the other parties.
As I sit in the House today I cannot believe that the NDP cannot contribute more to this debate. They should be rising to speak on this issue too. I think the reason they cannot do so is because they do not know where they stand on national unity. They do not know what the role of a national institution should be. When we hear more from them we will begin to understand whether or not they want to be a national party of purpose or just some rump group sitting over in the comer of the House of Commons.
These are very serious issues, not partisan issues. They are issues that we should all be addressing and we look forward to their contribution and I am sure that sooner or later they will have something to say. I look forward to the government being receptive to the amendments being proposed by our critic who has done a first-class job of bringing to the attention of all Canadians the importance of the CBC.

Mr. Speaker, I return to the subject of Radio Canada International which I brought to the attention of this House yesterday. I know that the minister was not able to be present yesterday but I did ask for serious consideration of the assurance that Radio Canada International be maintained as an integral arm and a broadcasting voice to the
international community as a voice of reason, a voice of a middle-western power, and something that the world scene requires.
It is not enough that the BBC, which is an important voice, or the Voice of America be heard, this middle power which is Canada and which is so highly respected across the land must also be heard.
I pointed out yesterday that CBC is in a very serious and difficult position because it is constrained. It cannot deficit finance, as the minister knows, and it cannot borrow.
I addressed my comments to the President of the Treasury Board, because in the final analysis the money that is allocated to CBC is determined by Treasury Board jointly with the Minister of Communications.
It is through their allocation of funds-actually through the starvation that they have undertaken of CBC- that we are, at this point, concerned about the maintenance of Radio Canada International as a viable voice of Canada to Canadians overseas and to countries that are looking for this middle level, democratic voice, that expresses cultural values in the two official languages here in Canada, English and French, and close to 1,400 other languages, which is an absolutely important function.
I have added this amendment because of our experience with the newly emerging democracies, the newly emerging democratic societies of this world who look to countries like Canada to understand democratic process.
I think that this House and the general public should know that the Speaker of the House of Commons asked that Mr. Philip Laundy be named as one of the officers of the House to enable Canadians and the Canadian democratic process to be understood by these newly emerging democracies.
Radio Canada International is in a similar position as the Speaker-the new one who is sitting there right now-and the Table Officers, men and women who in a non-partisan way help the instances of democracy work.
Radio Canada International is in the same position. The problem, perhaps, is that society does not understand the key role that is played by this service at a cost of $20 million a year to Canadians.
November 27, 1990

Not only does it bring a voice other than Saddam Hussein to Iraqis and Kuwaitis, enabling them to hear democratic views, it also brings the voice to our men and women who are soldiers playing a peacekeeping role on the front in many parts of the world.
I want to point out that 1990, which was a watershed year for freedom, came about in many ways because of the impact of voices like Radio Canada International.
I remember when we were discussing Tiananmen Square, we sat in this House until 3 a.m. Perhaps I was remiss but I thought it was very important to speak not only about the strength and the character of the young students who were in the square or the people's wish and hope for democracy. I spoke about the cameramen and the journalists who were in there bringing to the world a vision and a view so that we could understand what was going on.
At the same time, that voice-Radio Canada International-was bringing a picture of what was happening in that dynamism, in that moment of hope and then despair that was Tiananmen Square.
Mr. Speaker, the crumbling of the Berlin Wall and the changing dynamic in Europe did not happen without the voice of freedom that was heard on radio through short wave, through international voice.
It was very much the role of Radio Canada International. I wonder how many of us know that within days of the Tiananmen Square massacre, we began two daily broadcasts to China in Mandarin. We placed Radio Canada International material on local radio in three of the east European countries to which we broadcast already by short wave?
Through state broadcasts in Poland, Czechoslovakia and a private station in Hungary, all these countries were hearing the voice of freedom, the voice of democracy, the voice of a middle-sized nation, not one of the power brokers of this world, through Radio Canada International. These countries needed our voice. Now we are arranging training programs through Radio Canada International for nine broadcasters who are here from Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary on topics that range from journalistic policy and freedoms to the administration and sale of commercials, on how to bring the concepts of a democratic and free society together with advertising as a means of income for these stations.
Government Orders
We have had staff exchanges through Radio Canada International.
We have an incredible challenge through the international broadcasting voice in the Persian Gulf right now. I think many of my colleagues have alluded to what is going on in a very serious crisis that is at the flash-point in the Middle East. How can we hope that both sanctions will work and peace will come about because Saddam Hussein finally comes to his senses and realizes that you cannot just march in and repress another country? If his voice is the only one heard, how will the citizens start to react? Through the international broadcasting voice we can have an inside citizen understanding and we can work with the people of Kuwait and the people of Iraq and have them understand that our presence in that Persian Gulf is to enable a peaceful solution, not to become aggressors in war as a first step. If we do not sensitize, through a democratic voice, who else are they going to hear?
I am saying that when we put Arabic on the air in the Middle East we were rendering a very important service in the national interest. Although we contributed that $10 million to our forces, as our part of the $350 million that was being sought, we were still contributing to the development of the national interest and the national concerns of Canada and Canadians by explaining Canada's presence in the Gulf, by explaining the role of sanctions, by explaining why Saddam Hussein does not have the right to just walk in and trample on the people and the property of Kuwait.
Those are things that we can do so that we can emphasize the country's motivation in joining the multinational expeditionary force. We have made our airways available to Canadians so that Canadians could try to reach their families and friends in the Gulf area. We set up special telephone lines through Radio Canada International.
Radio Canada International has been very creative because it has not had the means needed to reach all these areas of the world. Although it does, with 14 languages through Montreal and then through their station in New Brunswick, broadcast to many parts of the world, in many parts of the world it has had to undertake joint contracts through Japan, through the BBC. It has been extremely creative.

November 27, 1990
Government Orders
I would like to really plead with the minister and say to him that he may not want to accept my amendment on the parliamentary channel to ensure that there is always the decision of the Speaker and the decision of this House in a non-partisan way. He may not want to ensure northern services. I think he is wrong, but he may not wish to. He may not wish to ensure all news particularly in French as well as in English as part of the CBC services, but certainly the international voice of Canada should be maintained. I plead with the minister to accept the amendment which was proposed, by the way, by a member from his own side, the member for St. Maurice. I would hope that we can see Radio Canada International enabled to be present on the international world scene because it could eventually be an even more important voice in the international voice for democracy and understanding across the world.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand in the House today to speak in the debate on report stage of a very important bill. The CBC has given this country the opportunity to reach across the globe for almost 50 years and convey to people what is happening in Canada and abroad. If I am not mistaken, I believe that we initiated CBC Radio International right after World War II. Our people in the Armed Forces were able to listen to what was happening at home and we were able to convey to them the message of support. We were able to convey to them that we at home are very supportive of their efforts and tribulations. Then, we went to the Korean War and our army overseas was again able to listen to the feelings of the people at home.
We have had peacekeeping forces for the past 25 to 30 years serving world-wide. In 1989,1 visited Cyprus where I had the opportunity to speak to a lot of our people who are there in peacekeeping forces. They related to me how important it is to be able to listen to Radio Canada International, the short wave of the Canada voice coming to them. It makes sure that we do not forget them, and makes sure that they can participate and be active Canadians while halfway around the world. They can understand what is happening here. The newspapers take about four or five days to reach there, but Radio Canada International can be there simultaneously, the same night.
We have something else which is important. That is parliamentary services of Canada. This government is notorious about a number of things. I say that, Mr. Speaker, n-o-t-o-r-i-o-u-s, "no Tory us". Why am I saying "no Tory us?" We have seen this government plummet to a 14 per cent rating. We are not sure if the government wants to chop off completely the parliamentary service because it does not want the rest of the Canadian people to watch what we are doing in this great House.
I have the opportunity from time to time to rise in the House and speak. My constituents come to me and criticize what I say or give me a pat on the back for what I say. I wonder if the minister sitting across-and I see he is nodding his head-also has the same from his constituents and most of his colleagues in government. We can see from the recent polls that at 14 per cent the government does not want this "no Tory us" nonsense broadcast. I would not be surprised for one single minute if over the next couple of months the proposals the government is putting forward to chop the budget, gut the CBC, is not done on purpose because and I quote: "476 Canadian cable companies have this as of March, 1989 and this is available to 7.7 million households".
My colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell also pointed out that the parliamentary channel should not only be available with a converter, but should be on a regular channel in French and English so that if people who live in the west want to watch it in French, they have the opportunity, or people in Quebec, if they want to watch it in English, also have the opportunity, or vice versa.
It is very important that we keep this service going because we have noticed that this government from time to time to time does not want the public to know what is happening. It wants to hoodwink the public, so it sweeps it under the rug.
I come to the next issue. Why the changes? Are we losing so much money that we want the changes? Are we going to privatize the CBC? Did I hear someone say yes? The minister is sort of nodding his head.
I go back to what we did with CN Express when we privatized it and gave it to Route Canada. The government was going to guarantee three years of service to our people. Eighteen months down the line, bang, we privatized Air Canada and 2,900 jobs were lost. We are moving to privatize Petro-Canada. I wonder how many jobs will

be lost? We are moving to privatize everything. I wonder, is the CBC going to be privatized next?
The minister says yes.

Ah, so there lies the culprit. We are going to move into privatization. Shame on the government, real shame on this government.
The other thing of great importance is CBC News-world. In September, Toronto lost the bid to have the Olympics in 1996.
It was a shameful decision.

My colleague from Eglinton-Law-rence says it was a shameful decision. I agree with my colleague because I am a Torontonian, but my heart also felt that the Olympics was eventually going to go back to its birthplace. It is something about celebrating the centenary. I was at a dilemma. What happened took me out of that dilemma.
However, it is important to note why the decision was made that the Olympics went to the United States. CNN was pumping directly into those peoples bedrooms and in their hotel rooms, scenes from where else? Scenes from Canada. Scenes about Oka and the turbulence with the Indians. It was also pumping into their hotel rooms the turbulence about Greece. We have seen how CNN effectively moved for them to get the Olympic games. Toronto lost and my city of birth also lost.
CBC Newsworld promotes national unity. There is no better means than having this opportunity for people, on channel 17 in Ottawa and on different channels across our country, to tune in through a converter box. Rather than requiring a converter box, this should be available on a regular channel so that Canadians can tune in and get more than a 20-second clip of what the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition said. I am sure they are not interested as to what the first said, but I am sure they are interested as to what the second said. Canadians have noticed that we go back to "No Tory Us." The people of this country are tired of listening to what the Tory government has to say. They tune in to CBC Newsworld and they watch with great importance. They look at the news that we have to provide. Yet this government, once it got CBC altogether in 1989-
Government Orders
Shame.

Shame, my colleague from Winnipeg says. In 1989, when the Tiananmen massacre broke, we were among the first nations to reach into mainland China with service in Mandarin and Cantonese and tell the people of China that we were supportive. We were among the first nations to reach and applaud the efforts of the students.
We are faced today with the situation in Middle East. We have approximately 2,000 servicemen in the Middle East. These servicemen watch with interest in what is happening in Canada. They watch and listen with interest to what we are doing.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you are giving me the nod that I have only a few seconds left. I am going to pose this question to the minister. I know it is going to fall on "No Tory Us" because of deaf ears.
Mr. Speaker, I ask through you, and I know the minister is not going to listen. Mr. Minister, what is your real purpose of this? Do you want to privatize CBC? Do you want to gut it, so it shows that it is making money, like you did with the post office and everything else? If that is the real thing, shame on them. This country wants no more "No Tory Us."

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to Bill C-40 which gives the government an opportunity to improve broadcasting services to the Canadian public and guarantee on-going parliamentary services of Radio Canada International, the Newsworld and the northern information services.
Our culture cannot survive without these services. Let us be mindful of the fact that Canada is not a uniform country but one where cultural, linguistic and geographical diversities play a very significant role. This is why the government cannot afford to miss this opportunity to maintain through legislation all the essential services of the all-Canadian CBC network. We simply cannot cut off the communication links which make it possible for Canadians to learn to appreciate their diversity.
Mr. Speaker, this government will be missing a great opportunity to enshrine in this legislation services that

Government Orders
the Canadian public both needs and wants. That is why I support the changes so eloquently put forward by the hon. member for Mount Royal.
It is clear that the Conservatives are backing down from recommendations that their own members supported in the sixth report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in 1987. Unfortunately for Canadians, it seems that this government refuses to listen to some of the progressive recommendations that come from the committees of this House. Mr. Speaker, as you well know, Canadians across this country have access to this place through one primary mechanism, the parliamentary service.
Canadians deserve a service to view their elected representatives in action. They deserve to have an unbiased and undisguised presentation of how their MPs perform their tasks. The challenge is to make certain that the new legislative framework and the funding arrangements will make adequate and appropriate provision for the full and effective use of the parliamentary service. Millions of Canadians who cannot come to Ottawa or who do not want to rely solely on media reports, tune in to watch us here in this Chamber. For more than a year, this service has been available to more than 80 per cent or 7.7 million Canadian households.
I firmly believe that it is worth while to legislatively ensure a continuation of this window on Parliament. May I add that I would be very interested to hear what objections the Conservatives have to this progressive amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this piece of legislation must cover Radio Canada International because its role has put Canada on the world scene. Other world countries have heard about us through this international network.
Radio Canada International came on the air in 1942 and the first network programs were heard in Europe in 1944. With respect to the international community, the RCI mandate is to reflect Canadian life and the various opinions which prevail in this country, not to mention various programs intended for Canadians overseas.
Mr. Speaker, Radio Canada International has a staff of 194 and listeners everywhere in Europe, Asia, the Caribbean Islands, Latin America, the Pacific, Africa
and the Middle East. At least 16 million listeners tune in to Radio Canada International programs on a weekly basis.
Nor can we ignore the fact that RCI promotes employment equity for linguistic minorities. Services in a wide variety of languages are a source of employmnent and contribute to promoting an ever widening multi-ethnic, multilingual and cultural society.

Mr. Speaker, this service has proved to be a beacon to countries which are emerging into democracy. Within days of the massacre in Tiananmen Square, when the Chinese pro-democracy protesters were suppressed, Radio Canada International began daily broadcasts to China in Mandarin. In October, the service switched to a full Chinese program service with two half-hour transmissions a day.
When a people are oppressed and when they do not have any source of information other than official government propaganda, services such as ours prove to be indispensable. They offer a ray of hope to a people who are starved for information. These people need to know that their struggle abroad is not forgotten.
I feel that this service deserves to be enshrined in the legislation.
It proves to be even more important now than ever. The situation in the Persian Gulf is critical. We have sent over 1,000 Canadians to a hostile area and have asked them to put their lives on the line for us. It is obvious to say that the need to have the service in the gulf is paramount. It is not only essential for our troops but for the people of the region to understand our true intentions.
For example, we should let the people of Iraq know that our quarrel is not with them but with Saddam Hussein. As we all know, effective propaganda on the part of the Iraqi dictatorship scewers the information that may be related to Canadian involvement in the region.
One must also remember that hundreds of thousands of Canadians at home listen to these broadcasts. They assist in promoting our multicultural and multilinguistic character. It provides a unifying voice for all Canadians, be they here or abroad. I respectfully submit that these
November 27, 1990

facts should help in convincing the government to accept Motions Nos. 12 through 15, as well as Motion No. 42.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation brought in Newsworld to provide news with a uniquely Canadian perspective. This channel gives a detailed review of events affecting all Canadians. However, it is disappointing that the service is only available in English. As a Quebecer, I think we should have this kind of services in French as well. I am sure this would lead to a greater degree of tolerance.

Finally, we cannot forget the fact that Canada is an arctic country. Our northern service is important to Inuit, Indian, Dene, Metis, and non-native groups. This service provides our northern citizens with programs in seven native languages. All these essential agencies must be preserved and protected within the legislation.
Liberals are concerned that this government is missing a chance to protect and recognize CBC services in this bill. I sincerely hope that members opposite consider the motions put forward by the member for Mount Royal and support them before passing this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for providing me with this opportunity to speak on a bill which threatens to do irreparable damage to our country's public broadcasting system.
Canada's history is rich and it is testimony to the strength of character and determination of our forefathers. In fact, without such a determination to be Canadian, combined with the guiding hand of government participation in a variety of sectors, Canada would definitely not have thrived nor asserted its national identity so strongly on the world stage.
This country is the fruit of the efforts and the will of our forefathers to build a nation east and west, to unite the land. Successive governments gave us a national railway system, a post office, a national radio and TV network, a national airline, as well as a variety of measures to help develop Canada as we know it.
Government Orders
If you look at what the Tories have done to the institutions I have just mentioned, you will be well on your way to understanding why the country is experiencing such an identity crisis and why so many Canadians have become so cynical about their government.
The privatization of Petro-Canada, the gutting of VIA Rail, the auctioning of Air Canada, and now the undermining of our national broadcasting system. All these policies were designed by a government seemingly intent on turning our country into an empty shelf. Frankly, I do not know how much more of this kind of mindless treatment our Canada can endure.
On a more positive note, Canadians have always been leaders in the field of communications, not only in telecommunications, but we have actually produced two world-class thinkers in communication theory. Harold Innis and Marshall McLuhan have set the standard as far as the study of communications is concerned. It would be an understatement to say that these two men contributed significantly to the affirmation of Canadian identity on the world stage.
It would be sad to see the progress we have made in this area come to nothing. I am amazed that the Conservative government has taken steps to undermine one of the pillars of of nationhood at a time when Canada is seriously questioning its raison d'etre.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the 1968 Broadcasting Act required that CBC contribute to the development of national unity. Unfortunately all reference to this has been eliminated from Bill C-40.
Moreover, the government's proposed broadcast policy stipulates measures which could, as the hon. member for Mount Royal has said, cause the disintegration of the national broadcasting system. The shortcomings of Bill C-40 which include the creation of two separate standing committees for English and French language broadcasting at the CBC, the failure to recognize various CBC services specifically, the regionalization of the CRTC, and the potential loss of federal jurisdiction will seriously undermine a system which has helped unite our country from sea to sea.

Government Orders
Although Bill C-40 is flawed, I believe that the amendments proposed by the member for Mount Royal go a long way in addressing and correcting its shortcomings.

Mr. Speaker, the amendments proposed by the Liberal Party, contained in motions Nos. 12,13,14,15 and 16, are aimed at ensuring the integrity of our broadcasting system. First of all, they would help the Corporation maintain its role of contributing to national unity and being a permanent expression of Canadian identity. Second, they would ensure recognition for and continuity of the following elements: the Parliamentary Service, Radio Canada International, the all-news service in English and in French and the northern Service. Motion No. 42 further refines the provisions concerning Radio Canada International.
Unfortunately, if the government does not act wisely and fails to approve the amendments we are proposing, Canadian broadcasting will be severly affected. And what about the unity of our country? If the Corporation is denied that part of its mandate which is to contribute to the development of our Canadian identity, one of the pillars of our collective consciousness will have ceased to exist.
Mr. Speaker, you will agree this is not the right time to approve such a policy. According to the government, this change in the 1968 Broadcasting Act is justified because the national unity clause would handicap the Corporation's ability to encure that its programming fully, fairly and accurately reflects and interprets the cultural, social, political, economic, linguistic and regional realities of Canada.
This does not stand up under analysis. In fact, Pierre Juneau, former President of the Corporation, stated before the Standing Committee that the phrase "national unity" did not cause him any problems during his mandate. In fact, the CRTC made it clear that its interpretation of this term had never hindered free political discussion.
The Liberal Party feels that the Corporation must maintain its contribution to developing national unity, especially at a time when Canada seems so divided. If Canada is to have and maintain a national identity, we must bring all regions of this country together and create
a feeling of belonging, and we can do through a well-shuchired broadcasting system.
Interestingly, even the chairman of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture supports the principle that the Corporation must maintain its mandate in this respect.

The minister has dismissed the CBC's 22-year old national unity mandate as intolerant interference, because the agency was maintaining this political value artificially and it was a constraint on freedom of expression.
I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, one of the more serious shortcomings of the bill. As we mentioned earlier, it fails to recognize various CBC services. If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention some of these services and highlight their importance.
The failure of Bill C-40 to recognize the CBC's all-news network in either English or French is extremely unfortunate, since we have seen that the corporation has made incredible progress in this area. I believe that this extremely innovative undertaking ought to be officially recognized.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, I come from New Brunswick which is the only officially bilingual province in the nation. English and French citizens have learned to live together in my home province. In many ways we have demonstrated to the rest of the country what biculturalism is all about.
It seems to me that the recognition of the CBC all-news network would be important and that it would help create and foster a sense of nationhood. Moreover, the development of a French all-news network would go a long way toward helping relieve some of the tensions which our country now faces.
As for the other services including the parliamentary service, Radio Canada International and the CBC northern service, I believe that the government should heed the advice contained in the 1987 sixth report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. It should provide these services with legal recognition in order to help forestall the possibility of abolition in times of budgetary restraint.
November 27, 1990

CBC is in a very difficult position at this time, as it can neither operate with a deficit nor can it borrow money. The minister well knows this. It is very important that the government and the minister put in this bill the power to guarantee the place for CBC and to guarantee its future budgets.

Mr. Speaker, I can see that it is approaching 12.56 p.m. I know that I will be stopping at 12.58 p.m. and will be speaking on this legislation after three o'clock.
I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Mount Royal on her amendment to the legislation, an amendment that we support whole-heartedly. We believe that those amendments are fundamental. They are very important amendments made in good faith. It is our hope that the government will take those amendments to heart and will deal with them accordingly-
As it has indicated before, the CBC is a must. It is not a luxury. It is not something that our society or our country can live without. CBC is a necessity for our society. It does not matter how we look at it, whether we are talking about our culture, Canadian unity, our history, the Canada that we want to build and see 15, 20 or 100 years from now, CBC always has been in the past and still is on the leading edge in promoting Canadian unity and culture.
We only have to look at Newsworld, as one example as my colleagues indicated a little earlier. That is one of the very few broadcasting institutions in our country where 90 per cent of its broadcasting is purely Canadian. That is something we have to pride ourselves in and to commend CBC on providing.
The second service is the parliamentary channel. I have been informed that over 7.7 million Canadians listen to the parliamentary channel on a regular basis. That is another very important service that is provided by CBC.
Of course that is not to mention Canada International, the international news system which we have in place. Nowadays, when Canada has an incredible, excellent and great reputation internationally, I think to turn around and shut down such an institution internationally would not serve our purpose or our country.
As many of my colleagues have indicated, we do support the amendment. I can see the clock approaching
Government Orders
1 p.m. At this point in time, I would like to commend my colleague on introducing those great amendments. I will be speaking on the bill a little later.

AFTER RECESS

Mr. Speaker, yesterday Canada Post announced that it is going to be closing the Yorkton post office on March 1, 1991.
Yorkton is a city of nearly 20,000 people, a trading area of some tens of thousands of people, and despite that this callous government across the way wants to close the post office.
I want is a justification from the government across the way as to why they it is doing it. I also want it to reverse that decision because if Yorkton, with at almost 20,000 people, goes, then what about the other towns and the other small cities across Saskatchewan and across Canada? How long is it before Kamsack, Estevan, or Weybum are closed as well?
The government across the way does not give a damn about rural Canada. I invite today the back-benchers of the Conservative Party to stand up and join me in a fight to save the Yorkton post office, to reverse that decision, to stand up for rural Canada, and to stand up for some of the historical values and contributions made in the

country by rural people. What is it doing to our rural way of life, to a service that people need, and a service that people want? Justify the decision and reverse it.

Mr. Speaker, there are many people on Rural Routes 1 and 2, Renfrew, Ontario, who wish that Canada Post would take their complaints about mail service seriously.
On October 1, Canada Post decided to award one contract for the two rural mail routes to a person who does not live on either route. Canada Post unceremoniously dispensed with two well-liked and efficient contractors who knew everyone along the way. In return, it gave the people a service where cheques and other types of mail were ending up in neighbours' mailboxes; letters that were put in mailboxes for the contractor to pick up were left in the mailboxes; a businessman lost the opportunity to bid on a contract because the tender was floating around in the system; and wrongly delivered letters that were put back into the mailboxes with instructions as to where they belonged were being delivered back into the same mailboxes a few days later.
Customers on RR 1 and 2 Renfrew want me to call on Canada Post again to treat their legitimate complaints seriously, to review the contract that was granted on October 1, to talk to the customers about the type of mail service they are receiving and to get this serious problem settled now.

Mr. Speaker, my compliments go out to the federal and provincial ministers of agriculture who recently agreed in Winnipeg to several initiatives recommended by agri-food policy review task forces.
One in particular will lead to the creation of an agri-food advisory council for environmental sustainability. This council will advise ministers on resource base and environmental policy issues for the agri-food sector. This is one element of a three-part strategy relating to the conservation of soil and water and the protection of the environment. The strategy will also involve the
private sector which will advise on programs in each province relating to the sustainability of agricultural resources.
Hon. members anxiously await the ministers' next meeting scheduled for Februaiy when they will assess the situation following the conclusion of the GATT negotiations and discuss the cost-sharing formula of the proposed safety net system.

Mr. Speaker, we can see that the GST is already hurting our economy. For example, under the GST transitional rules all industries, except the housing industry, will get rebates for inventory on hand at December 31, 1990.
With new housing, purchasers of homes started prior to that date will qualify for an FST rebate of 2.8 per cent of the purchase price if they close before February 15, 1991. They get nothing after that date. All inventory standing as of December 31 carries the full FST and is subject to full GST if unsold by March 31. That inventory will suffer a double taxation.
A high interest rate policy and a phenomenon of walk-away purchasers are exacerbating that problem. Those in housing propose one simple, corrective solution. Specifically, will the Minister of Finance extend the deadlines for the FST rebate provisions, or will he allow builders the same rebates available to purchasers, following the March 31, 1991 deadline?

Mr. Speaker, the concept of regional development is frequently misunderstood by many Canadians, particularly those in regions who do not require such help.
We must always remember that Canada is a confederation of regional distinctions, some of which have economic advantages over others. One principle of Confederation is a fair balance between regions so that economic advantage and disadvantage are equalized.
All too often, regional development is characterized as charity. Nothing could be further from fact. Regional

November 27, 1990
S. ft 31
development is a right in Confederation. That is why the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is so crucial to the Atlantic region. It is a program of fundamental economic advantage to these four provinces, which is designed to provide the potential for economic balance with more affluent regions of Canada.
It is not only important that we maintain ACOA's advantage, it is even more important that we use it wisely and well to create lasting benefits which, themselves, will help achieve the balance and may, eventually, even remove the need for special regional aid. Until then, regional development is a unique and essential instrument of Canadian Confederation in Atlantic Canada and elsewhere.

Mr. Speaker, we are appalled by an article in The Ottawa Citizen today which denies the suffering endured by Inuit of northern Quebec, who were relocated to the Canadian high Arctic in the 1950s as part of a government initiative. It is obvious that the writer has not spoken to any of the Inuit involved, nor does he have any personal knowledge of the circumstances and hardships which confronted these Inuit people.
The writer accuses the survivors and descendants of the relocation of spreading garbage. Perhaps this writer, unlike the people who were relocated, never had to forage through a white man's dump because he was hungry.
The article is misinformed, ill-researched, and pompous. Not only do these Inuit people deserve recognition of their suffering and an apology from the Canadian government, they now deserve an apology from the writer of this disgraceful article.

Mr. Speaker, from December 3 to December 7, International Trade ministers from 100 or so GATT member States will meet in
Brussels to conclude the Uruguay Round and make decisions on the future of world trade. This Round is the most ambitious one we have known since 1948.
The Union des producteurs agricoles in Abitibi- Temiscamingue has made frequent representations during the past few months. It is afraid the Canadian government's strategy consists in gaining access to international markets for our wheat in exchange for dropping subsidies and production support programs in Eastern Canada for milk, beef, pork, and so forth.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian representatives must stand up for our farm producers in Quebec and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday, in La Presse, we were again treated to one of those recycled statements by "Lord Screech". Premier Clyde Wells was at it again, and all I can say is that although as Quebecers, we patiently listened to him for eighteen months when there was still hope for renewed federalism, today, our patience has run out. We will not stand for lectures from the Premier of Newfoundland on citizenship or Politics 101, Mr. Speaker.
The Premier of Newfoundland had the nerve to say that the Belanger-Campeau Commission was unlawful. Mr. Speaker, we have news for the Premier. The Belanger-Campeau Commission will serve as a guide for all Quebecers in deciding on their common future, and nothing Clyde Wells can do will stop them. Quebecers have nothing to learn from " Lord Screech" who says today it is up to the federal government to decide on our future.
Mr. Speaker, the right to self-determination is internationally recognized. Even Newfoundland called a referendum to decide whether it would join Canada. And today, they would deny us the same basic right? Mr. Speaker, that is unacceptable!

Mr. Speaker, today 12 different housing interest groups are on Parliament Hill lobbying for continued support for co-operative housing by the federal government.
They want the federal government to make a commitment now to continue direct sponsorship of the index-linked co-operative housing program in 1991 and beyond. The income mix as it now exists in housing co-operatives has been developed over the past 20 years and allows people from different economic and social backgrounds to build strong, healthy communities together. The index-linked mortgage has significantly lowered the cost of developing non-profit, co-op housing. The current program costs 58 per cent less in the first year and almost 20 per cent less over a project's life than the previous program.
As the Federation of Canadian Municipalities' Big Cities Mayors Caucus has put it, it urges "the federal government to maintain the federal non-profit co-op housing program with the existing income mix component".

Mr. Speaker, more on NDP hypocrisy.
I am deeply concerned about both the Ontario New Democratic Party and their federal cousins here in Ottawa. It seems that they are unable to decide in which direction they are headed. Simply put, they do not know which end is up.
One example is the Ontario government, headed by back-flip Bob, who have reneged on a majority of election promises. Now these self-annointed environmentalists have proposed to extend the already overburdened Keele Valley Dump site, thus threatening the Oak Ridges Marine.
What makes this situation comical is that the federal NDP is putting forth a candidate claiming to be an environmental engineer, if you can believe it, in the York North by-election where the dump is located. This type of confusion is consistent with NDP policy-making.
After all, the party to my left is where Big Bad Bob received his political training.
A second example of confusion politics is the NDP stand on constitutional reform. It has managed to cover all of its bases with a federal leader who states that she is a federalist, her entire Quebec caucus which believes in sovereignty-association, and a provincial leader who has absolutely no idea where he stands.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am truly worried about the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, the gulf crisis is not an issue over which Canadians should seem to be divided.
It would seem that it has become the pattern of politics in the country that the opposition is not prepared to agree with the government even on the time of day or the weather forecast.
But Canadians cannot seem, nor should they be, divided on the actions of a Saddam Hussein. We cannot seem to be divided over the actions of a nation that arbitrarily invades its neighbours, or a leader who is prepared to use his nations' children as cannon fodder, or to gas his own troops.
The world is united against such actions and is preparing to send the message that such behaviour will not be tolerated, indeed will be repelled with force, if necessary.
Canada must stand unequivocally with our allies on this issue, and Canadians should stand united.
I urge all members of the House to put Canadian and world interests first, to lay aside their partisanship, and show Saddam Hussein and his ilk that their actions are totally unacceptable to Canadians.

Next week, Mr. Speaker, the representatives of 100 countries will meet in Brussels, Belgium, to seal the fate of international trade. For Quebec farmers and dairy producers, this round of GATT negotiations is one of the major indicators of the economic future of the whole agricultural community in Quebec. Since the mid 1980s

Oral Questions
the United States and the European Community have been waging a costly war to market their agricultural products, a war whose annual tab amounts to $300 billion in financial support of every description.
Mr. Speaker, I urge our govemement to remain firm at the negotiation table so that our agricultural producers may keep what they have acquired through many years of efforts and sacrifices.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, my riding of Dartmouth is home to many of the men and women who are currently serving under three Canadian naval ships, HMCS Alhasbaskan, HMCS Terra Nova and HMCS Protecteur which have been deployed in the Persian Gulf.
It is also home to the families who have been left behind while their loved ones go off to an area of the world in conflict. To say that these people-wives, husbands, children, parents, and friends-are living through a stressful period of time would be an understatement.
Fortunately, they do not have to wait in isolation. Thanks to the work of the Military Family Support Centre, under the direction of Lieutenant Commander Tom Willdey, they have been strengthened through the establishment of special Ships Spousal Support Networks for each of the ships on deployment.
It is a chance for the families who have been left behind to get together and get involved in activities, to be updated on Gulf news, or simply to enjoy the company of someone with whom they share a similar experience.
The idea of the Ships Spousal Networks is not new. They often come about when a vessel is away at sea. However, under these circumstances these networks are special and participants are describing them as a lifeline.
Thanks to the work of Lieutenant Commander Willdey, the staff, and volunteers at the military family support centre, these life lines remain strong. For that
the families, the community, and members of all parties in the House of Commons thank them.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, a few veterans in my constituency were left with the mistaken impression that they would be adversely affected by spending cuts included in the supplementary estimates. I have discussed this matter with the Hon. Gerry Merrithew, Minister of Veterans Affairs, and am pleased to tell those veterans and the House that they will not be touched as the Department of Veterans Affairs finds $3 million in reductions.
For instance, there will be no reduction in budgets for disability pensions, no reductions in war veterans allowances, and no reductions in the Veterans Independence Program. The cost of transport for counsellors to veteran clients will not be cut. No cuts are being made in the operation of the veterans' hospital or veterans' homes. Reductions will only apply to operating and capital budgets so veterans in Calgary and across the country will not be adversely affected by spending cuts.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Canadians are aware of a draft resolution currently under discussion among members of the United Nations Security Council. This resolution would authorize all necessary means to get Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait on or before a deadline, likely this coming January 1 or January 15.
Yesterday, speaking from the Middle East, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, and I quote: "My personal view is that deadlines are artificial."
Will the Prime Minister confirm that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was speaking for the government when he said that deadlines are artificial?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution to which my hon. friend refers contains the words "draft resolution" because it is just being considered by members of the Security Council. It demands that Iraq comply fully with Resolution 660 and all subsequent relevant resolutions and decides, while maintaining all of its decisions, to allow Iraq one final opportunity, as a pause of goodwill, to do so.
I think that the Secretary of State spoke about what all members of the Security Council who seek peace and who seek the respect of the Security Council resolutions and not war, have been addressing. The pause of goodwill would be sufficient to allow the President of Iraq another opportunity to reflect upon actions that he has taken and to do what the world community unanimously has called upon him to do, namely, to withdraw from Kuwait and to return to the borders of his own country.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has not denied that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was speaking for the government when he said that deadlines are artificial.
Therefore, I ask the Prime Minister: Has the government instructed its representatives at the United Nations Security Council to inform the other members of that council that Canada will not support a deadline being included in the draft resolution on Iraq currently being discussed among members of that council?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I have indicated very carefully what the Secretary of State for External Affairs is seeking to achieve, and it is consistent with the participants at the Security Council who on every resolution, of which this will be the eleventh, have supported almost unanimously the requests that the authority and the moral authority of the United Nations be respected and defended. Yesterday, for example, by way of illustration, it is reported that Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev delivered an ultimatum to Iraq last night warning it to withdraw from Kuwait or face the worst consequences. "If Iraq really wanted to settle within the entire region and is interested in avoiding the worst, it must now openly pull out
Oral Questions
of Kuwait and release hostages, " Gorbachev reportedly told Foreign Minister Aziz.
President Gorbachev said: "He must weigh everything once more. The fate of Iraq is now in the hands of its own leaders and time is expiring". Indeed, this is the language and the substance of the resolution. Time is indeed expiring. What Canada is seeking is the opportunity for the President of Iraq to weigh this very carefully and to make a considered decision, such as the one that President Gorbachev yesterday invited him to make in the interests of world peace.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all welcome the interest of President Gorbachev in peacefully resolving this matter.
I did not hear any deadline mentioned in the quotation from President Gorbachev read out to the House by the Prime Minister. The UN resolution does make a specific reference to a deadline.

Speaking to an American Senate committee this morning, former American Defence Secretary James Schlesinger said that so far economic sanctions against Iraq have produced the expected results but might have to be maintained for a whole year if they are to have a decisive impact. His opinion is shared by a good many international affairs experts.
My question to the Prime Minister is this: Does he share the views of these experts and, if not, would he explain why?

Mr. Speaker, sanctions do have an impact on Irak, and this is why the Canadian government approved them and support them with the troops that have been sent to the scene.
Nothing in the resolution proposed for the consideration of Security Council members flies in the face of that reality. However most council members see eye to eye on one point: if the president keeps insisting, they might have to consider other circumstances and other options. But that is as far as the resolution goes. Nothing there clashes with the position taken by the Canadian government, or those of the President of the Soviet

Oral Questions
Union or of the President of the French Republic, to name just a few.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague just said, according to many observers there is strong evidence that sanctions are working.
It would seem important to listen to further evidence concerning sanctions from our parliamentary delegation now in Iraq. We would like further clarification and to know if the Prime Minister agrees today that sanctions still are the best means to achieve UN goals and a resolution of the conflict in the Gulf?

Mr. Speaker, we are there in the gulf because we seek to avoid war. We seek to defend the interests and the integrity of the United Nations. We seek to assist in the deterrence of aggression which is consistent not only with our traditions and our history, but also with our position as one of the founding nations of the United Nations.
Indeed, we believe that sanctions have played and will continue to play a useful role. There is nothing in the draft resolution at variance with that.

We have three people in our office. They have three people in their office. They have their office budget like we all have. Each MP has that. They have that.
This Parliament has been very liberal-small /-toward the Bloc quebecois. That is what my constituents say.
They have places in this House. They have been asking questions. They have been allowed to get in the House after a questionable oath taking ceremony. We have been very liberal.
It is not a party. It does not have 12 people. Those are the rules. They should stop whining. The House has been very liberal to them and I find it shocking when they get up and whine, bitch and complain.
If my constituents were here in the House, they would be a lot harder on them than the rest of us. We have been very liberal toward them. They should stop whining and get to work by using their existing resources.

I am going to exercise my prerogative as Speaker and take the point that the hon. member for Shefford has made. I see other members rising, and this could go on all afternoon.
It may well be only an administrative matter, but the hon. member has argued his case with some passion and I am going to consider it carefully.
I am going to return to the House, and I hope my response will at least show that the complaint has been taken seriously, which I know the hon. member wishes me to do. I hope that my response will be consistent with fairness in the House.
This is not a place to continue a debate on oaths or other things.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-40, an act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

Motion No. 17
That Bill C-40 be amended in Clause 3 by striking out lines 39 and 40 at page 5 and substituting the following therefor:
"(vi) contribute to national unity, shared national consciousness and identity",

Motion No. 30
That Bill C-40 be amended in Clause 5 by adding immediately after line 6 at page 9 the following:
"(a) establishes priorities for the system based upon the national interest;"

Mr. Speaker, this is a very crucial amendment to the bill, perhaps to one of the most important parts of it. Let me summarize what it does.
The 1968 Broadcasting Act, the act that we are changing, says that part of the mandate of the CBC is to promote national unity.

Government Orders
The government has removed that clause from the CBC's mandate. This is a very crucial change to a bill.
In describing the CBC's mandate, this present Bill C-40 describes it as follows: That the CBC should:
(i)	be predominantly and distinctively Canadian,
(ii)	reflect Canada and its regions to national and regional
audiences, while serving the special needs of those regions,
(iii)	actively contribute to the flow and exchange of cultural
expression,
(iv)	be in English and in French, reflecting the different needs and
circumstances of each official language community-
(v)	strive to be of equivalent quality in English and in French,
(vi)	contribute to shared national consciousness and identity,
(vii)	be made available throughout Canada-
(viii)	reflect the multicultural and multiracial nature of Canada;
And so on.
Yet, the government has removed the one obligation from the CBC, that of promoting national unity. The removal of this clause combined with the division of the CBC board into English and French standing committees weakens the CBC as a national institution. It seems to me that now more than ever we need someone to speak for Canada. We need to start looking about strengthening national institutions.
My hon. friend from the Bloc quebecois wants to dismember Canada, to have a separate Quebec and other separate regions in Canada.
There are forces in the country that are out to destroy this very country. There are traitorous forces in the country that want to dismember it. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the government itself should be moving to strengthen national unity, not to weaken the country; to strengthen national institutions, not to weaken them. That is what is happening in this bill.
Marjorie Nichols, my friend, writing in the paper today, The Ottawa Citizen, suggested that maybe we should privatize the CBC. Well, there again, we would lose another national institution. The people in the country are asking who is speaking for Canada. They are dying for someone to speak for Canada. Look at the opinion polls. They want someone to speak for Canada.
Steven Godfrey, in a recent article in The Globe and Mail, put it this way: "The proposed changes," that is, the change in dropping this clause out of the Broadcasting Act, the promotion of national unity, "are a sad commentary on the fact that there remains no area in which the very words 'national unity' can be spoken without inviting attack from members of the federal government alone. The federal government itself."
In an earlier speech today, I pointed out how the government is leeching the CBC by cutting back its budget and by relying more on advertising revenues to make it more of a commercial corporation. The government is squeezing and leeching the CBC. What is it doing now? It is meeching the CBC.
Oh, oh.

I make reference to Meech Lake. What the government is doing is saying we want the CBC to have a Meech Lake view of Canada, but Canada is a little more than Joe Clark's community of communities. This is one reason why ordinary Canadians were opposed to Meech Lake. It is not because they were anti-Quebec, not at all. That is a misinterpretation in Quebec.
My friend laughs and many Quebecers believe that, but it was not to be anti-Quebec at all. Canadians believe, I think, that there is an over-all Canadianism that is beyond the regional loyalties and Canada must be more than 10 distinct societies. It is true that Quebec has a special place in Confederation, through language and culture, and should have power to do that.
Canadians, by and large, when they think about it, including English Canadians from all over the country, agree with that. But they do not want to see a number of decentralized distinct societies in the country so there is no national government at all. That is what this government is doing. That is what this Prime Minister tried to do with Meech Lake. That is why Canadians rejected that. There is a greater view of Canada.
When I was speaking in the Meech Lake debate, I said-and you have to remember that goes back a few years, Mr. Speaker-that Canadians do not want Team

Alberta with Gretzky-he then played for Edmonton- or Team Quebec with Mario Lemieux-he was then playing for a Canadian team. They wanted Team Canada. They wanted to see one team and they wanted people to speak for Canada.
The minister and others have expressed the view that keeping the clause dealing with the CBC promoting national unity will lead to propaganda, that the CBC will be forced to maintain an artificial, political notion of unity in defiance of the artistic integrity of the corporation and the independence. The minister noted in his speech that Liberal governments in the past have launched witch-hunts against separatists in the CBC. That is wrong. Clearly, it is wrong.
It should be noted that the CBC's journalistic independence is protected elsewhere in the bill.
I see the minister leaving the House. I hoped the minister would stay and listen to this very important clause. He just puts his hand down and he leaves. It is one of the reasons why this minister has never got this bill through the House of Commons and why it is being delayed. He just does not simply care.
This is a key provision of the bill. The government has attacked the CBC in the past. It stacked the board of the CBC. It made political appointments, such as Bill Neville and Elizabeth Bumam. It has cut back the budget of the CBC. It attacked people in the last election campaign. Dale Goldhawk, for example, the president of ACTRA, was silenced and forced to resign his union position. It has taken after other people in terms of the investigation of election coverage in respect of the free trade issue. Look at the attacks on Roy Bonisteel and David Suzuki?
The CBC is in trouble. The CBC has problems. Part of the reason is because of this government. It is about to attack the CBC radio. I appeal to people out in the country who are followers of CBC radio and CBC television, when it is at its best, to stand up for the CBC and to stand up for Canada. Do not let the government destroy it. My God, it has destroyed almost everything we have got. It has taken our rural railways and our rural post offices and gotten rid of them. It has cut back railways. It is about to sell Petro-Canada. It has slavishly followed the United States in foreign policy. We are losing Canada. This whole country is up for grabs and this is an indication of what is going on. This country may not survive.
We are in a struggle for survival in the next couple of years. This government should be forced to go. It is too bad that we have this out-dated system where a government can be so low in the polls and at the same time still have a majority in the House of Commons, because we have gutless back-benchers who are afraid to vote against their government. If they were not afraid, we would not have the GST. We would not have the cutbacks in these national symbols.
The government is removing the national unity clause of the CBC. It has said to the CBC board of directors: "Well, now you have to sit in English. You have to sit in French." The next step will be while there will be an English network and a French network. Then there will be an English network responsible to the government in Ottawa and a French network responsible to the government in Quebec. Then there will be two countries. We are moving to lose Canada. We need people to speak up for Canada and we need these particular clauses.
I know there are arguments saying that the CBC should not be a propaganda tool. I do not believe the CBC is a propaganda tool with government. I think there are problems with the CBC. I think some of the commentators, as Rick Salutin said in the Saturday Night article recently, feel that perhaps there is too much centralized power in Toronto where the CBC broadcasters, such as the Peter-and-Wendy-and-Barbara group, take on too much power to themselves.
But the real view of the CBC is an instrument of national unity, reflecting Canadians to Canadians, taking every part of the country and showing it to other parts of the country, not being a commercial network, such as the American networks, being distinctively Canadian with 95 per cent Canadian content in drama, with a Canadian view of the world, reflecting to our people.
Who speaks for Canada, Mr. Speaker? Not the government. Who is going to stand up while this country is going to the dogs? I hope ordinary Canadians will put pressure on the government, hopefully to get it to resign and to change government in Canada.
I believe this country is worth fighting for. I believe we are losing it and I think that is a great tragedy. We have to fight it everywhere we can and this is one of the places to fight it. I am pleased my colleagues in the other
