We want to see the role of the CBC to promote national unity. We want federal institutions to speak for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to thank the hon. member for his excellent presentation.
I am glad that this review of the Broadcasting Act provides us with another opportunity to talk about national unity. To me and to millions of Canadians and Quebecers, this question is extremely important, and I think it is a matter of utmost concern. I therefore want to take every opportunity to express my faith in a country I am proud of, a country that is mine, that is ours, and a country that is admired and respected throughout the world. Tell me: Where on this planet would we be better off than right here in Canada? Unfortunately, we are destroying this country with a bill that is a disaster, that is poorly drafted and unacceptable to Canadian men and women.
It should come as no surprise when I say that when I read the papers or watch television in Quebec, I can't help wondering who defends the interests of Canada in our province. There is plenty of talk about sovereignty and independence, but hardly a whisper about federalism. I am reminded of what was said so eloquently by the leader of my party. My leader said it this way: "No one has the courage to talk about Canada in Quebec," and I think this is very sad.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, my leader said no one has the courage to talk about Canada in Quebec, and I think he is right. And that is why I object to the abrogation of the national unity clause as proposed by Bill C-40 before the House today.
The bill, in fact, does away with the mission entrusted to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in 1968, and I quote:
Contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a
continuing expression of Canadian identity.
If we relieve the Corporation of this obligation, who will take over that responsibility? Isn't the corporation the nerve centre of our communications, as was said by our Prime Minister? What do we expect to accomplish with this wording change proposed by the government, for it does not add anything-quite the contrary, it diminishes the importance of the CBC mandate? There can be no doubt that at a time when our country has to cope with profound divisions concerning our constitution and linguistic issues, at a time when intolerance and racism are all too often so obvious, the CBC can indeed be the very link which unites Canadians from coast to coast and which can promote our identity and set off the absolutely unique nature of our nation.
Since the infrastructure is already in place, Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why we should fail to ensure that it is properly maintained and in good condition. Why would anyone want to thwart such positive measures and not promote national unity? I cannot understand that.
Can this kind of mission be considered as propaganda, as the Conservatives claim, and I quote my leader, Mr. Jean Chretien:
The raison d'etre of a country is to survive.
Quebecers have to be told about Canada. Never since
Confederation has the survival of our country been so seriously
threatened.
Even after the Meech Lake failure we must continue to cultivate the will to live together, to understand one another, and to respect, support and appreciate all our differences. We must put the emphasis on the similarities which unite us, not on the differences which divide us. By taking away from the CBC the mandate to promote national unity-and not the Union nationale, as our Minister of Communications said a number of times in the House, for he thinks we are still in the mid 1960s-are we going to prevent the broadcasting of scenes which do nothing at all for national unity? If so, I will come back on my position.
As I see it, changing the words will not change anything. Freedom of the press would always be respected, and I sincerely hope so. I have in mind the sad isolated incidents in Brockville and Sault Ste. Marie which, repeatedly shown on the screen, led us to believe that all English Canadians were intolerant, something

which our history has contradicted on a number of occasions. That is unacceptable.
I suggest that the government is making a serious mistake by weakening an institution such as the CBC, which is the cornerstone of our broadcasting system. As far as the government is concerned, the CBC should be relieved of its responsibility for national unity at the time when the government should be using eveiything at its disposal to ensure that the people of Canada are well informed and share a common vision of the future, while appreciating our regional and linguistic differences.
I believe that building national unity in Canada requires developing its character, building its identity and its national conciousness. We need strong institutions like the CBC to ensure that all regions and all social partners weave together the fabric of national unity.

Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this is not the way this bill is designed. What this government is doing is building a form of sovereignty association into our national broadcasting system, the CBC, instead of building bridges of communication and common links across this land. Cultural survival is one of the critical issues today.
I have before me an interesting piece of legislation which is presently being looked at by the European council. They have set up an important fund called the Euromidges support fund. It was set up at the end of 1988 to develop the European cinematographic and audiovisual industry. Its main aim is of a cultural nature. It said in its report that the importance of audiovisual works in transmitting European culture in all its forms is obvious. The European cultural values in particular to younger generations must be communicated.
Cultural survival is a critical issue today. Broadcasting is a central vehicle through which Canadians can communicate, a major instrument for Canadian expression in the arts and entertainment, an essential means for providing a Canadian perspective in news information and programming. CBC reaches almost every household, so it is in a unique position to enable this cultural appreciation and growth as identification for ourselves, our children and our grandchildren. This is what will
Government Orders
help form Canada and inform Canada. It becomes a very distinctive culture on the global map.
I find this whole approach totally disturbing. On the television sets in our living-rooms is this little remote control that my grandson calls "the little clicker". We hold the key to the future of the cultural identity of Canada. If you look at this bill and if you look at the way the government has put a sense of sovereignty association into this bill, it is totally disturbing. It has taken the CBC and divided it into English and French. It has taken the national unity mandate away from it. It has taken the CRTC and balkanized it by putting in a "he who hears decides" on a regional level. It has put in the potential for a challenge of its federal jurisdiction through its definition of programming.
This bill is totally unacceptable and the national unity clause is the greatest farce of them all when you see what the government has done in removing that. It has also removed all the other things that make this a distinctive Canadian unity from coast to coast and have allowed us to take a sovereignty association vehicle, instead of being the central nervous system of this country, the transportation unit of the intellect. We have managed to destroy a wonderful concept that needs to be reinstated into this country.

Since the House is dealing with Bill C-40, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my views on the two amendments moved by my hon. colleagues of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party and aimed at using the CBC in part as a propaganda agency.
I know that the Hon. Member for Mount Royal would simply love to see the CBC become an exponent of her own political convictions, that her leader would love to appear more often on the CBC and feels that the CBC should act as a agent of his party. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that if we respect the freedom of the press, the creative ability and the record of an institution which has adequately served its listening and viewing public, I do not think that we should allow the CBC to become a propaganda agency.
The NDP member has emphasized that the CBC should-

Weaken Canada!

Government Orders

He said: "Weaken Canada". I say to the hon. member that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would have no credibility if it were to become a propaganda tool. I am surprised these members show so little respect for the intelligence of the audience.
Mr. Speaker, you yourself were once a dynamic element of Radio-Canada, and I am sure you would never have wanted to become a propaganda tool. This particular clause in the Act could be interpreted very narrowly. If tomorrow morning, the hon. member for Mount Royal became minister of Communications, I predict she would immediately tell the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation about his obligation to promote national unity. And in any referendum we might have in Quebec, for instance, Radio-Canada would play a proactive role that would have no connection with the neutral and objective information gathering to which Radio-Canada has always been dedicated.
The hon. member said earlier that we did not talk enough about federalism, that not enough people were talking about it. The problem isn't Radio-Canada. The problem is that the hon. member can find no credible spokespersons for her option in Quebec today. Only her leader, on his occasional visits to Quebec, mumbles a few words about old-fashioned federalism. But we shouldn't blame Radio-Canada.
What we must realize is that there are no more credible Francophone spokespersons for the option they want to suggest, no one who is prepared to serve their cause, and that is true across the province. When I see this abdication reason and common sense, these demands for a propaganda mandate for a Crown corporation, I can tell them it won't work. Quebecers didn't give Radio-Quebec a mandate to work for Quebec's sovereignty. In fact, the first people to object would have been the hon. member for Mount Royal and all her friends in the Equality Party. They would immediately draw parallels with the Nazis or whatever. We have heard those speeches before.
Why do they want to make Radio-Canada do something they would not approve in the case of Radio-Quebec? When the Parti quebecois was in power in Quebec City, for instance, did they tell Radio-Quebec: Now you are going to pursue the same objectives as the government? Never, Mr. Speaker! They had too much respect for freedom of the press.
When I heard the hon. member for Mount Royal say that the leader of her party said a country's purpose in life was to survive, I thought I never heard such a stupid statement. A country's purpose in life, Mr. Speaker, is to share what we have and to establish common institutions. Survival is not enough. When I hear them saying this sort of thing, I am not surprised they have dropped substantially in the polls. They just want to survive, but we want more that just survive, we want to live! To that extent I believe that the definition she wants to give to the CBC again underlies the weakness of their arguments.
Mr. Speaker, they say that the CBC should develop a common vision of the future, but who will do that? The hon. member for Mount Royal, or perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver? Will it be Clyde Wells, Mr. Speaker? Can you imagine Clyde Wells being the CBC president tomorrow morning? What kind of propaganda outlet would it become?
Hear, hear.

I see the Liberal members applauding. I can appreciate that, Mr. Speaker, because they may already be looking for a new leader and Clyde Wells seems to be giving a much better performance than their present leader. Even so, Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to promote him.
When I hear the kind of statements Clyde Wells has just made, suggesting that the Belanger-Campeau Commission is illegitimate, can you imagine what it would be like if he were president of the CBC! He would ban all news concerning the B-C Commisison. When he states that the future of the country lies in the Senate, it speaks volumes for intelligence and democracy! You know, Clyde Wells is the one who is called- In fact he is the Premier of Newfoundland, the man with great ambitions. He is learning French not only to be able to speak on the CBC English network, but now he also wants to speak in French on Radio-Canada!
He is not a New Democrat.

He is not NDP, but NDPs are worse, Mr. Speaker.
The point I wish to make is that instead of asking the CBC to do the job for them, they should offer true alternatives to Quebecers. I respect their determination to promote federalism and Canadian unity. I tell them
November 27, 1990

that we are prepared to discuss this issue with them anywhere and anytime.
Over the past few weeks, Mr. Speaker, debates were held in 26 Quebec CEGEPs, and in most cases, the elected Liberal members did not have the guts to appear before the students. They had to send in their some insignificant party hacks. I can tell you that my friend from the NDP and my colleagues of the Bloc Quebecois took part in these debates. We did not ask the CBC to do our own job. The fact is that these people are desperate, that they cannot find anyone to transmit their message and they would gladly avail themselves of the federal government's resources.
Mr. Speaker, that happened before and I must confess that literally at the time the Canadian Unity Information Centre dumped millions upon millions of dollars on Quebec. A gentleman named Paul Tellier was in charge then but now the situation is different; such abuses were tolerated in the 1980s but today they would be totally unacceptable.
And I say to the Federalists: Go ahead, promote your convictions, but do not try this time to use Ottawa's spending power to buy the support of Quebecers. You would simply fail. Every effort to buy their support would result in a massive rejection. It is not without reason that the vision defended by the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada only has a mere 6 per cent support in Quebec. This is not CBC's fault but that of the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada himself, with 6 per cent. Even if he appeared every night on the CBC television network, he would not convince anybody. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say to them: Do not try using federal taxpayers' money to put one over. Use the power of your convictions. The time for propaganda is over!

Mr. Speaker, it is a relief to get up to speak. I can only say that the unmitigated balderdash to which we have just been treated by the hon. member for Shefford needs some response, even if it does dignify such nonsense by even mentioning it.
I am enthralled by the clear belief that the member who just spoke has absolutely no regard for journalistic integrity, obviously no regard for the professionalism of journalists who work for the CBC, and clearly no regard
Government Orders
for journalists in general. I am glad to see the hon. member for Halifax West applauding. I trust that the hon. member for Halifax West holds the view I do. I would presume he does, that Canadian unity is a good thing. Perhaps he does not. No doubt he will have a chance to say so himself.
It is a tragedy in this country today that people are asking from one coast to the other, east and west, north and south, inside Quebec and outside Quebec: "Who speaks for Canada". When did it become a crime in the minds of members of this Chamber to speak out in favour of Canadian unity? When did it become some sort of disgrace, to quote the member who spoke previously, some propaganda, to be in favour of the survival and the flourishing of this country?
I cannot believe that anyone who would sit here in this House, who would stand in this House and speak or claim to speak for Canadians, could actually stand and argue against Canadian unity. It is a sad time that we have come to, if this is the case in this country today.
The mandate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for Canadian unity is something that has been with us for a very long time. It is something that the past president of the CBC, Pierre Juneau, said did not in any way interfere with the workings of the corporation in serving its various and multicultural audience.
On May 16, The Ottawa Citizen reported that the CBC is an agent for Canadian unity. It must remain that way as a bulwark against various decentralizing forces. Everybody who sits in this Chamber knows what the decentralizing forces are. There are hundreds of them. There are the questions of language, culture, geography, and regionalism which every single one of us in our home provinces and here in Ottawa have dealt with and continue to deal with on a daily basis.
The things that pull us apart are part and parcel of our experience as Canadians. They make us who we are. To quote Andrew Coyne in The Financial Post, "they make us know that we are us, that we are imperfect and that we have a multitude of problems", but they also make us know that we have survived for 123 years and, please God, we will survive as long as this earth survives. Mind you, with this government, that may be a problem as well.

Government Orders
The member who spoke previously talked about a mandate for national unity destroying a respect for creativity. I am sorry that my colleague for Kingston and the Islands is not here to make his usual interjection of "what nonsense", because that is what it is. It is rank and errant nonsense. The creativity that has been fostered by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation across this country, whether one is talking about Cod Co. from the province of Newfoundland or cultural programs that relate to our native peoples in the north and in the west or whether-
Codswell.

It is codswallop, just so that the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte will know.
At any rate, the cultural programs which have come from all over this country reflect that "useness", if I may coin the word, that is Canadianism, that is neither English nor French nor any of the multitude of other cultural groups of people this country. It is Canadianism.
When I speak to that, I know that I speak to the hearts of millions of Canadians, from whatever background they have been fortunate enough to spring. I know that that strikes a cord. It must strike a cord in the vast majority of members of this House, because this country in all its works and pomps is perhaps the most precious gift which any group of 26 million people were ever lucky enough to receive.
We stand here in this Chamber, we look at a Crown corporation such as the CBC, and we know that that Crown corporation, that broadcasting network, has made a difference to Canadians all over this country. It creates for Canadians a sense of self and a sense of oneness with our neighbours. The forces that pull us apart, as I said before, are many, varied, and strong, so we must be particularly careful of those forces that pull us together, and the CBC is one of those forces. It is something that Canadians, certainly those of my generation and the generation that is coming behind me, have always taken as a given. I say that of Canadians, of whatever background and of whichever of the two official languages.
I recall, as a graduate student in England with other Canadian graduate students from Quebec, Ontario, the maritimes and the west, staying up all night to listen to Radio Canada International in order to get the news
from home, to listen to hockey games, and to just keep our link with our home country. That is how we discussed it, English and French, of whatever background, our country. It remains our country. CBC is one of the strongest mechanisms that makes it stay our country.
This summer I was fortunate enough to travel to different parts of Canada to speak to friends and family who live all over this vast country. I visited Quebec, western Canada, and the north. I heard the same thing from all these people. What is happening to our country? What has become of the country that we all fought for? What has become of the spirit of tolerance, acceptance and acknowledging each other?
I will tell you one of the things that has become of it, Mr. Speaker. It has become the butt of jokes for people who have no respect for the history and the traditions that began with great explorers who came to this country in the winter with De Monts and Poutrencourt who came to Port Royal.
My friend over there thinks this is funny. He thinks that a spirit of caring for this country is funny. I am glad I amuse him. If I amuse him, that is fine. He should remember that French and English alike have a stake in this country and will hold that stake. It is this country. It is not two countries; it is one country. It is not two nations; it is one country.
I fear for my colleagues in the New Democratic Party as well. The critic for the New Democratic Party, the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, said in a November 25 article in The Toronto Star that he does not share the fears of the member for Mount Royal about the deleted national unity clause. He believes that the CBC contributes to unity simply by existing.
I believe that it contributes to unity simply by existing. I believe, along with the member for Mount Royal, along with the member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, and along with every Liberal member in this House, that putting in the mandate for national unity can only strengthen that endeavour. It can only strengthen our belief that this is one country of many peoples, all with an equal share and an equal stake; that we are not going to see the CBC die; that we are not going to see that mandate destroyed; and that we are not going to see this

country go down the tubes because of an irrational response of a government that does not care.

Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about the stand taken by the hon. member for Mount Royal who is in fact attacking the freedom of the press. I get the feeling that she has the same disease as her leader who accused members of the press of being against him. In his view, to be on his side, journalists have to be actually working for him. She said we should promote national unity because there is more talk about separatism than federalism in Quebec. But that is what is really happening in Quebec, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, there are more people talking of sovereignty than there are talking of federalism. Should the CBC not reflect that fact, make it known and ensure that the people get a clear picture of what is going on in Quebec? Should objectivity be denied for the sake of national unity?
Should the CBC be used for propaganda purposes? What would you say if Radio-Quebec were used to promote sovereignty? That is not the case. That is not the mandate it was given by the national assembly.
Mr. Speaker, for the hon. member for Mount Royal national unity means that you must say "Jean Chretien is against Meech Lake!" if you are speaking English, and Jean Chretien est en faveur du lac Meech if you are speaking French. That is how the member for Mount Royal sees national unity, Mr. Speaker.
Does national unity mean that the people of Quebec are to be made to believe that the NDP exists in Quebec because it exists in British Columbia? Come now! We know that would not be an objective statement and that is not the truth. So, once again, the CBC must reflect the reality and not be a propaganda tool at the hands of the government.
Must we, all in the name of national unity, display Chinese vases, would say a very contemptuous former prime minister as he did when he was having problems with Quebec? Is that what national unity means for the Liberal member? All in all, if the people of Quebec make use of the CBC and pay for it, do they not have the right to be informed objectively? Do francophone journalists not provide objective information? I am almost done, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that there is a

disinformation problem in Quebec at the present time. It has to do with anglophone media distorting the Quebec reality and not informing the rest of the country of what is going on. All Quebecers do not live in the town of Mount Royal, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to join in debate at report stage of Bill C-40, an act to amend the Broadcasting Act.
The legislation before us is similar to that bill which was presented in the House before I became a member in 1988. Because the election was called, of course, that bill died on the Order Paper.
As a former broadcast journalist, the major difficulty I have with this bill, and indeed the Official Opposition has with Bill C-40, is that it drops the CBC's 1968 mandate, and I quote, "to contribute to the development of national unity to provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity".
I have always found, and I am sure other Canadians agree with me, that the CBC has been a great instrument of national unity and, in fact, an expression of our very identity, the promoter of our cultural distinctiveness, our linguistic duality, and our regional diversity.
Government Orders
Where there are no CBC affiliates, there is a tendency to rely on news provided by American networks which have the budgets and resources to post correspondents around the world. The result is, of course, good news and good reporting, but it is through the eyes of another country, a country very different than ours, with a different philosophy and a different ideology.
There was the courage to establish a national broadcasting network composed of radio and television outlets across Canada, in part to resist the strong cultural influences of the south.
While working as a television broadcast journalist in the city of Barrie, Ontario, CKVR, a CBC affiliate, was fortunate enough to rely in part on news gathered from across the country and around the world. Then, while employed by CHCH-TV in Hamilton, Ontario, it became quite evident to me, because of budget restrictions and because it was an independent station-that is it did not have an affiliation with the CBC or CTV networks- we had to rely on our international news and purchase that news from NBC. The American slant to the news was ever-present, and that cannot be denied. The same can be said of other news organizations from across the country. Instead of relying on the American feed, they would be able to broadcast news from a Canadian perspective, with Canadians speaking on Canadian issues from around the world about those issues important to Canada.
Part of the reason behind the national unity clause was that Canada was so vast a land and in many ways geographically remote, that it was necessary to bring Canadian content to these regions. Many people wonder what the true identity of Canadians is. Whatever the definition is, as our communications critic for the opposition, the hon. member for Mount Royal noted: "there is no doubt that without a constant and unflinching determination to be ourselves and the direct and constant involvement of our government, never would we have survived or would we have preserved our identity."
This bill would move the CBC away from that mandate of promoting national unity. Just because the CBC is well established does not mean that it has to turn its attention away from its national unity role. After all, the forces of the United States are not any weaker today than they were yesterday. Indeed, they are even stron-

ger. Make no mistake. By opposing the changes to Bill C-40, we are not fighting against outside influences but fighting for our national unity. At this time in our nation's history, the role of national unity and our national broadcasting network is especially and crucially important. As other Canadian institutions are put on the auction block or are disseminated by this government and decimated by this government, such as the massive VIA Rail cuts that we saw last year, the CBC is truly the purveyor of national unity and is that thread that weaves and binds the regions of our country.
Unfortunately, it appears that the damage the Conservative government has wrought on this country is not enough and is far from over. Now it has sets its sights on the CBC. What is next? Privatization? I would certainly hope not.
Speaking on the record, the second reading of the Broadcast Act, 1932, R. B. Bennett stated of the national unity mandate that: "This country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources. Without such control broadcasting can never become a great agency for the communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thought and ideals. It seems to me that in Canada, the system we can most profitably employ-''and the members opposite perk up their ears when they hear the word profitably-R. B. Bennett was talking about cultural profitability, "is one which responds most directly to the popular will and the national need."
He concluded: "In this stage of our national development we have problems peculiar to ourselves and we must reach a solution of them through the employment of all available means." The Minister of Communications said of the national unity clause that it is an "intolerable interference" because the CBC "was maintaining this political value artificially and it was a constraint on freedom of expression."
The minister himself has not contributed greatly to the CBC's freedom of expression when he himself has cut an estimated $240 million over six years. How can the CBC pursue the mandate it was founded to perform when it is under siege by this government? The maintenance of a
Canadian broadcasting system such as the CBC is fundamental to the future of Canada.
Most people recognize how greatly affected we are by what we hear and what we see in connection with radio and television programming. Statistics brought forward in earlier debate by the hon. member for Mount Royal, who has been very articulate and worked very hard on this very thick bill, show that 80 per cent of our publishing industry rests in foreign hands. Eighty per cent of our publishing industry rests in foreign hands. Ninety-seven per cent of films shown in Canada come from outside the country. Eight-five per cent of records and tapes are based on imported master tapes in broadcasting. Seventy-one per cent of all programming viewed by English-speaking Canadians on television is American. The figure is lower in French-speaking Canada.

Canadians watch an average of 24 hours of television programming each week and 18 hours listening to the radio. Obviously, these statistics reveal not only how we rely on radio or television for entertainment, but show us how whatever is actually being broadcast will make its impression, affect our thinking. It is therefore important that the CBC remain an agent of Canadian unity and that it is so described in this legislation.
I would like to address a couple of other amendments put forward by my colleague, the member for Mount Royal. The amendment is grouped together with that of the amendment of the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, dealing with the national unity cause itself. This amendment, Motion 17, reaffirms the mandate of the CBC to:
"(vi) contribute to national unity, shared national consciousness and identity,".
This clause must be put back into the legislation. I believe that these amendments and others put forward by my colleague for Mount Royal will address some of the inadequacies of this bill, especially the one dealing with national unity.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take just a moment to participate in the debate here this afternoon because I must admit I have been disturbed somewhat by not only what I have heard, but the way in which it has been put.
I think that most of us who have been in political life for a little while understand that the basics of it all is communication. If your constituents cannot talk to you, reach you or tell you what their problems are, you cannot very well solve them.
It seems to me that part of what I have heard discussed here this afternoon has to do with that ability to communicate. It may be that the CBC is only one of many ways in which the people of Canada can talk to one another. But it is apparent from the debate this afternoon that if we need anything, we need an ability to talk to one another.
I do not know that it serves a useful purpose to have a nation split up, people unable to communicate with one another, with political parties forming in different regions of the country and the rest of us not even able to share in that discussion.
It seems to me that some of what we have seen this afternoon is evidence of that, that there are political parties forming and reforming in this country which have a different idea. It would be fine if we all had some means, like this Parliament and like a national communications system, to hear them out, to hear what they have to say and to respond to them. It seems that some members do not want to hear what others have to say. They do not want to accept that somebody else might have an opinion just as valid as theirs.
Government Orders
I would argue that in this bill and in this Parliament this afternoon, there is evidence that we have a major problem in just translating our beefs to one another. I think we better resolve that because I think that that is the road to ruin. Whether one would be a member of the Bloc quebecois arguing that no one else in the world understands their point of view, or whether somebody is from the Reform Party in western Canada, and somehow you feel that the rest of the nation has not bothered to listen to you, we should all admit that at the very least we need a means to communicate. We need to resolve some of our difficulties and disagreements. If we have an argument that is real and substantive and divides, then surely it should be something where we can sense, but not just that we forgot to talk to one another. It is not just that we did not have any means to communicate. It is that the question before us is for real and that the arguments are for real. They are not because someone portrayed us in a light that we did not want.
It is difficult in this day and age where communication very often is not the long speech that is made in this Parliament, but communication is a 20-second clip on television. I do not think that any of us could deny for a moment, whether we like it or not, that we have all seen clips of life that have had much more impact on the people of this country than anything that has been said in this Chamber.
I think, very dramatically for example, we are now getting around to the point where we are analyzing the clip of people in the city of Brockville, Ontario, who walked on a Quebec flag. Now we are analyzing how widely that visual was disseminated around the world, and how much of an impact it had on people in Quebec, in other parts of Canada, and in other parts of the world. It is dramatic. It is ironic that it was the CBC which had the thoughtfulness to go back, almost a year after the fact, and analyse is that really what those people were trying to transmit? Well, most of them were not even from Brockville. Most of them did not have that idea in mind when they participated in something that was captured in a small video clip and broadcast around the world. That is the negative power of communications.
What about the positive power? Is there a chance? I was struck again during the entire Meech Lake debate of how little Canadians know about one another, about the different circumstances in which people in Canada find themselves. I heard this afternoon in this chamber a lot of members who, it seems to me, simply feel that if someone could slip a few words into a piece of legislation, the problem would be resolved. I do not believe

that is true. I wish it were that simple, but I do not think it is. I have heard members espouse that if we could only find a new slogan, or a new person, or a new leader, that all of a sudden all of the nation's problems would disappear. I do not believe that is true either. I wish it was, but I do not believe it is.
I look at the world, particularly a nation like Canada, and it is a pretty awkward place to tiy to govern. I am sure even the Prime Minister would admit to that this afternoon. It is difficult to bring together all of the different regions of the country. Some times people would say "this country does not make sense. It is too big. It is too diverse. It is hard to get around. It is cold. It is not a friendly climate in many parts of this country".
In part, even old Tories like Sir John A. Macdonald understood some basics about this nation, that if you wanted to be a nation people had better be able to reach one another. They need a train to go from one place to another, or you cannot even pretend to be a nation. People would have said: "You need things like a post office. You have to be able to send letters to one another". Even if you do not send a whole lot of letters, there has to be something which represents the federal government in each of our little communities. That is not a supermailbox. That is a tradition which they call a post office. They recognize that as being a focal point for the federal government in their community.
If there is someone who is undermining all of this sense of a nation, it probably is not anyone on this side of the aisle. I do not think that I would point my finger at less than a dozen members who purport to be something called a Bloc quebecois. I would look across the aisle where someone has taken away most of the institutions, slowly, surely and methodically, over a fairly lengthy period of time on which people have relied to make this a country that works.
Part of what we are discussing this afternoon is, once again, someone looking to the CBC to solve all their problems. I do not think it can. I do think it ever has. I do not think it ever will. But, I think it is part of what we need. If there is not an effective communications system in this country, how can you even have the argument? You cannot. You will wind up with people shouting
slogans. That does no one a service, no one anywhere in this country. It is difficult. Many of the members here have had a chance to travel across Canada. The first thing that hits one when one tries to do that is that this is not easy; this is a huge nation, a diverse nation. We need to be able to talk to one another, we need to communicate effectively, we need to reinstate all of those institutions that brought us together, in the first instance.
I think it is sad, but it is a fact, that this government has moved steadily, slowly, on a day-by-day basis, to take away some of the things that made it possible to have a country called Canada. It seems to me, and it is evident from the discussion this afternoon, that the nation called Canada has a crisis on its hands, not just one but many of them.
If we are to move forward in a sensible, rational manner, we will need every communication device we can conceive of, including a revitalized Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to do that. I believe it is possible for all of us, with very different ideas about what this country should be and about what the problems are here and extremely different ideas about how you would resolve them, to meet somewhere, whether it be by means of radio, television, print journalism, an effective communications system, or a postal system that we can all recognize in our own community. If these things can be put together and if members here and all Canadians can have some chance to utilize these things we will have, at least, an opportunity to work out our differences.
Part of what disturbs me about the debate I have heard here this afternoon is not that people argue and disagree but that they have no time to hear someone else's point of view. You cannot win an argument that way. One can shout people down; one can avoid the eventual resolution of a problem; but one cannot win an argument unless one is, first and foremost, prepared to hear what the other side has to say. One must test the waters and see if the grievances of others can be addressed. There has not been a lot of that in here, this afternoon.
It is true, as I have heard members say during the course of this debate, that this nation is changing. I am not sure that it is a planned, logical evolution but, undeniably, it is changing. It is changing in economic terms, in linguistic terms, and in demographic terms. I would hope that in this Chamber and in the broadcasting done by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, we

would at least have an opportunity to have a sensible, rational, logical argument and that we could, at least, have the tools that would allow us to communicate, effectively, with one another. I hope that that is what comes out of this bill and other attempts by the government, but I must say, I do not see a concerted effort to do that. Quite the contrary, I see things moving in the opposite direction.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me this afternoon.

I want to make a few comments on what my colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa, said earlier. His concept of Canada probably parallels that of quite a few people in this country. Bill C-40 deals with amendments to the CBC act. My colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, put the problem into perspective.
What I would like to do in the time allotted to me is to point out, perhaps, some of the good things that emanated from the old Bill C-136, which are now incorporated in Bill C-40 and also, as gently as I can but hopefully with constructive criticism, point out where the bill might be a little bit deficient.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, said, the purpose of Bill C-40 is really to replace the 1968 Broadcasting Act and is essentially identical to Bill C-136 which died on the Order Paper when the 1988 federal election was called. The legislation had its genesis in the task force on broadcasting policy and it had an extensive review by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, which resulted in four reports, containing recommendations for new broadcasting legislation. Since Bill C-136 died, we hoped that the new minister would take the time to reshape a new bill and put his own imprimatur on it. In my opinion Bill C-40 is not such a bill. It is still the hurried bill of a defeated minister with very few changes. We had hoped that the new minister and the Department of Communications would have prepared a report on all of the suggestions made by so many responsible citizens and
Government Orders
groups, by so many experts and, at the very least, explained why their concerns have not been met.
I mentioned earlier that there were positive provisions which were carried forth from Bill C-136 to Bill C-40. Among them, we the Liberals are very pleased to see the following provisions. Women, children, cultural minorities, aboriginal peoples and the disabled are specifically mentioned in the legislation. The need to portray more accurately the multicultural nature of our society is also included in there. The special nature of the French language broadcasting environment is recognized. The CRTC will thus be required to take these market differences into account when making licensing decisions.
The originators of program signals and their authorized agents, such as the cable operators, will be able to take action in the courts against commercial pirates stealing their scrambled signals. There is provision for making educational broadcasting an integral part of the law. I want to deal more specifically with that particular area a little later in my speech.
Local Canadian stations will be given priority status when carried by cable, and the provision that the president of the CBC be a member of the CBC board of directors seems to be a very common sense approach to this whole thing.
There were some amendments made by my party which were accepted in the legislative committee, such as the recognition of community broadcasting as one of the elements of the Canadian broadcasting system, along with the public and the private. We are going to have an amalgamation of the three. The mandatory requirement that the Canadian Broadcasting system be owned and controlled by Canadians is just common sense. Why should we have our communication systems controlled by someone outside this country? The programming of Canadian broadcasters will also include children and be a reflection of the multicultural and multiracial nature of Canada, ensuring that television and radio more accurately portray the multiracial as well as the multicultural nature of Canada.
Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to interject a few mild criticisms, if I might, hoping that with these interjections the minister will perhaps consider them. We believe, as I am sure my hon. colleague from Manitoba believes, because in his heart I believe he harbours Liberal ideas, that Bill C-40, while improved, is still seriously flawed

Government Orders
and should not be passed into law without further major changes. We believe in a national broadcasting system and a national vision of Canada; not a community of communities, not two Canadas, and most definitely not 10 Canadas. Bill C-40, if passed, will only further separate and Balkanize Canadians at a very critical point in our nation's history.
The following are some of my concerns. First of all there is the challenge to federal jurisdictions. We in my party are concerned that the federal government's jurisdiction over broadcasting could be challenged through new definitions. The new definition of broadcasting in clause 2 of the bill is defined broadly as to include the transmission and reception of programs other than by means of radiocommunications; that is to say, hard wire or closed circuit transmissions. These were considered previously to be under provincial jurisdiction.
Second, undertakings will be divided into programming and non-programming functions, a rejection of the conventional legal practice which has regarded such undertakings as indivisible. That too seems to be absolutely in keeping with common sense.
My colleague who is sitting beside me, the member for Hamilton West for whom I have a great deal of respect, addressed the problem of Canadian unity. The 1968 Broadcasting Act required that the CBC "contribute to the development of national unity". Of course it should. It is not there for the unity of another country. It is there so that we can speak to one another as Canadians. However, that reference has been dropped in Bill C-40. Why would they do this if this is the major raison d'etre for this bill?
I skipped a lot of what I wanted to say because I want to deal with the educational service. First, the alternative program that we talk about in education should not be introduced at this time or through Bill C-40. This ruling was expressed by the Nova Scotia Department of Transportation and Communications and the Canadian Association of Broadcasters to which my colleague belongs.
However, if the government believes that there should be another service, we believe that it should be a Canadian learning channel which would address national needs while serving provincial and educational demands of its learner audiences. A Canadian service would provide a necessary and needed complement to the already existing American learning channel, which in 1987 was watched by 120,000 Canadians. That was an increase of 124 per cent over 1986.
There is a dire need to put forth our own Canadian programs for Canadians. Liberals recognize that education is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. We feel that collaboration by the provinces should be encouraged to provide such a service. Issues and social challenges such as the general criticism of current educational standards, emphasis on the delivery capacity of education in Canada and others would be countless subjects available for the exploration of Canadian learning in this country. We should have our own learning channel.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by thanking the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting, all 21,000 of the them across Canada who brought this issue forward in the years between 1985 and 1990. They worked extremely hard to bring this issue back before the House of Commons.
The Liberals, and myself personally, believe in the goal of Canada in developing its national personality. Building its sense of national identity and consciousness are factors needed to build Canadian national unity. This has been endorsed by my colleague from Quebec when he spoke on behalf of the Bloc quebecois. He and I do not share the same concept of Canada. We need a strong, national institution like the CBC, as my colleague said, to weave all the regions together in this mosaic that we keep talking about, the mosaic of Canada.
In my riding there is approximately 486 Friends of Canadian Broadcasting. Many of them have written to me on this issue, trying to bring to my attention to the many important aspects of Canadian broadcasting. I am in total agreement with the thrust of what they wrote to me about, and here I am before the House speaking in support of national unity as part of the CBC mandate.
If we look back to 1932, when the government of the day decided to create the public radio service that eventually became the Canadian Broadcasting Corpora-

November 27, 1990

tion, at that time the government made a very important step. It realized that Canadians should have control over broadcasting in Canada. R. B. Bennett said at second reading of the broadcasting bill, as reported at page 3035 of Hansard of May 18, 1932:
First of all, this country must be assured of complete Canadian
control of broadcasting from Canadian sources-
He recognized that Canada's autonomy and independence hung on the control of our communications systems.
When television was introduced, there was a need for further regulation to protect Canadian content and culture in CBC programming. Therefore in 1968 a new Broadcasting Act was introduced, at which time something very important took place. At that time the mandate of the CBC was to "contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity". For the first time in Canadian broadcasting history, the national role of the CBC was reaffirmed.
The CBC realizes that Canada is unique in both its demographic and cultural diversity. As a result, a national medium is required to serve the needs of the Canadian population. Precisely because the CBC is considered our national medium, it does not make much sense to eliminate its role to promote and preserve a uniquely Canadian identity. As we know, traditionally the CBC has been a great vehicle for promoting Canadian culture.
There is no doubt that there is money to be made by decreasing Canadian made programs and by purchasing low cost commercial production, but the facts remain that Canadians without a doubt enjoy the CBC the way it is. I have the figures to prove it.
Nearly 500 English radio outlets and almost 200 French radio outlets broadcast CBC services in Canada. This year the CBC's annual report states that English and French radio programming reached about one out of five Canadian adults every week. That is approximately six million Canadians on a weekly basis.
As for television, English broadcasts are now made from 18 stations, 23 affiliates, and 637 broadcasters. CBC French television is broadcast from 217 media outlets. During the year 1988-89 television season, the CBC
Government Orders
English audience share was 17 per cent, a figure that put it on par with the three major American commercial networks in their home markets.
The fact that the CBC has almost 20 per cent of the television market share is very impressive, particularly since most large cities in Canada receive all the American channels and some Canadian stations broadcast American programs.
The figures show also that Canadians are watching more and more Canadian television productions. According to the CBC annual report, efforts to Canadia-nize prime time schedules of both English and French television networks have had positive effects.
For instance, since 1984-85 the production of prime time CBC English viewing captured by Canadian programs rose from 60 per cent to 64 per cent. For the French network, for example, the proportion of viewing to Canadian programming has risen from 75 per cent to 85 per cent. Clearly the CBC continues to be a leading force in bringing a uniquely Canadian flavour to broadcasting in Canada. There is absolutely no reason why this should not be mandated within Bill C-40.
There can be no doubt that in this day and age we are flooded with information from all sides. It is for this reason that Canada needs a national information clearing house to sort through the information and present it from a Canadian perspective.
The CBC has always been a unifying force for Canada. It should be allowed to grow and continue to be Canada's voice. I do not think that keeping the national unity clause within Bill C-40 will turn the CBC into an instrument of the state, as has been stated by some members of the House.
Looking at the past four years, the CBC had some really difficult times. For instance, when the government was first elected in 1984, it promised support for CBC's resources and independence. However, in 1984 when the Minister of Finance introduced his mini budget, the first thing it did was cut $75 million from the CBC parliamentary allocation.
The following year, in February 1985, the first advertisement of the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting appeared in The Globe and Mail, calling upon the Prime Minister to study the future of broadcasting instead of making senseless cuts to the CBC's budget. In May 1985

Private Members' Business
the government responded by appointing the Caplan-Sauvageau task force on broadcasting policy.
The following year, after extensive public hearings and research, the task force issued a comprehensive unanimous report with recommendations for broadcasting policy and a badly needed new Broadcasting Act.
In 1987 a House of Commons committee studied the Caplan-Sauvageau report and issued unanimous recommendations to the government supporting the thrust of the task force report. As a result, in June 1988 Bill C-136 was introduced and in September 1988 it died on the Order Paper.
Now we have Bill C-40 before us. I would like to stop right here by saying that we do support certain aspects of the bill, but we would whole-heartedly like to see the government adopt the recommendation of the hon. member for Mount Royal.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the two or three minutes remaining to express some of my views on Canadian unity.

I am pleased to speak about the unity clause because what we are talking about is the essence of Canada. The best statement I have heard or read to date comes from the The Financial Post a few months ago. It indicated, and I quoted: "If information is the currency of commerce of the modem economy, ideas are the binding force of a modern nation. We can no longer be defined by what we are but by what we believe. To be Canadian should mean to stand for something".

So we must leam and appreciate the fact that the CBC can be used as a vehicule to express the concept of Canada. We can defend Canada only if there exists a concept which all people can appreciate.

On that question, unless we give the CBC the opportunity, the mandate, or the requirement to gather together all concepts which in their totality define Canada and Canadians, identify the regions, and show the contribution that each and every one of these regions
gives to the Canadian identity, both on a cultural and linguistic basis, then truly we can say that we have a vehicle for the expression of what is Canadian.
Unless we consider the amendment that my hon. colleague for Mount Royal has presented, we will forgo the opportunity to give the CBC not only this mandate but the opportunity as well to carry out the concept of a Canada that exists in the totality of all of its residents and all of its regions, be they from the west or the east, from the maritimes, from Quebec whether they speak French or English, or from a culture like my own which fits into neither pattern.
The important reason to support this amendment- and I think my colleague from Shefford can also appreciate it-is that we cannot understand and fully integrate the total diversity that is the essence of Canada, unless we are willing to recognize specific regions.
One would be tempted almost to say the distinctive nature of certain regions can be translated and exchanged with all other Canadians through a common vehicle. We are going to forgo that opportunity. For what purpose? To give us an opportunity to turn our backs on fellow Canadians? To ignore the contributions that French and English-

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE ON ABORIGINAL PEOPLES IN FEDERAL CORRECTIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of immediately implementing the recommendations respecting policing of the Thsk Force on Aboriginal Peoples in Federal Corrections, as presented to the Solicitor General on March 30, 1989, and file with this House a timetable for implementing the remaining recommendations.
November 27, 1990

He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion was placed on the Order Paper many months ago when I was the critic for our party in the area of the Solicitor General and dealt with federal corrections.
Under the system in which the House operates, the names of members get drawn to present their motions. Mine happened to be drawn. I was very pleased about that and for the opportunity of presenting this motion to the House, because I view it as a particularly important motion at this time.
The issue of the condition and treatment of our aboriginal peoples is a matter that, of course, is now front and centre in Canada, one that has attracted the attention of all Canadians over the last number of months. The problems have been with us for many years, and the problem in particular of the treatment of our aboriginal Canadians in our corrections system is one that has been before Canada for years and years.
The Solicitor General's department and the Correctional Service finally responded to those problems with the appointment of a task force on aboriginal peoples in federal corrections. The task force was, for practical purposes, internal to the Correctional Service. Its members included Mr. Ingstrup, the present Correctional Service of Canada Commissioner, along with Messrs. Rayner, Nuttall, Sawatsky, Cunningham, Louis, and Dicemi, as well as a working committee, all the members of which came from within the Public Service of Canada.
The task force reports and recommendations outline the continuing horror story and the sheer racism of the treatment of native and aboriginal Canadians within our corrections system.
As we all know and as it has been pointed out time and time again, it is a scandal that a so-called civilized country such as Canada should treat its native people the way it does. There is no clearer picture of the discrimination against native people than the treatment within our Correctional Service.
It is a story of institutional, systematic racism, institutional conservatism, and an inability to change and respond to an obvious wrong, immorality, and evil. There is the simple statistic that 9 per cent of those within our Correctional Service who are incarcerated in Canadian
Private Members' Business
prisons are native people. Yet, they only reflect 2.5 per cent of the general population.
To some extent, the Correctional Service of Canada can say: "Well, that is somebody else's fault. We only take the ones they send us." Yet, as this report shows, native people stay in jail longer than white, non-Indian, non-aboriginal inmates in our system. They spend less time on parole and more time actually behind bars. They have fewer services available to them. Frequently, their religion is given no regard whatsoever. Their system of thought and of internal government is disregarded and the result, of course, is that it contributes to recidivism among the native populations in Canada.
The time has finally come for the House and for the government to address the issue and to procrastinate no longer. The government, through the Correctional Service of Canada, produced a fine report, full of excellent recommendations. As a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General, when I asked Mr. Ingstrup, Commissioner of the Correctional Service, what he intended to do about implementing the report, he said that there was a committee working on this. This was over a year ago, I think in the spring of 1989, shortly after the report was made public.
I am quite looking forward to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General telling us specifically what has been done to implement this report. If he is able to say that there has been substantial implementation, then I will congratulate him. But I would also hope that the parliamentary secretary will come to the House and offer a timetable for completion of implementation. I would hope that not only will there be a substantial record of achievement over the last year and a half, but for those items which have not yet been implemented, that a timetable will be offered today in this House.
This is not a partisan matter. It is a matter on which all sides of the House can join. We want the parliamentary secretary and the department to come forward with accomplishments in this area, because the people of Canada finally are saying to the government: "Do not wait longer. You must act on these recommendations."
I could take the House through the recommendations. They are important, but it seems to me the important point to make now is that the time has come for action.

Private Members' Business
There is a companion report which appeared after I had filed this motion in the House. That report is called Creating Choices, and it is the report of the task force on federally-sentenced women, filed in April, 1990. Among women who are incarcerated, there is again a disproportionate number of native people. This report poignantly outlines the pain that is suffered by native women in our prisons. Just recently, there was yet another suicide, that of a young native woman in our prisons.
I know that the Solicitor General has responded very positively to this particular report and he is to be congratulated for that. He recently announced that finally after over 50 years, the prison for women in Kingston is going to be closed. He said that the government has made a firm commitment to implement the recommendations of the task force on federally-sentenced women. I would like to hear from the parliamentary secretary a specific commitment to implement the recommendations respecting native women in our prisons, because that is important to hear and it is important to get the government on record on that.
We have not yet heard in the House the government commit itself to an implementation of the earlier task force report on aboriginal peoples in our federal corrections system. I would ask the government to take this opportunity to deal with this long-standing and painful issue. I would ask that the parliamentary secretary take the time to outline the specifics of what the government has done and what the government will do.
I am going to keep my remarks brief, because I know there are other members who would like to speak to this. I call on the government, not only to speak to the issue, but to allow this motion to pass unanimously before six o'clock.

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE ON ABORIGINAL PEOPLES IN FEDERAL CORRECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the reference to policing was just partly Freudian as a result of the member's fine work on the Committee for Justice and the Solicitor General where the hon. member for Victoria served over the last year or so.
In any event, the task force report that is the subject of the motion raised many issues in corrections at a time which was well in advance of a number of very public Canadian events that brought to the attention of the public our clear delay in addressing a number of very obvious needs of native Canadians, not just in the field of corrections, but in a broad spectrum of activity that cuts right across the whole of their existence. We, in Parliament, must share some of that blame.
The task force was not a parliamentary task force, but was a task force of individuals with expertise in the field that was being studied, that was corrections.
The recommendations of the report address very clearly and succinctly a number of areas to which I am sure we agree the corrections system should be responding. I will mention just a few of the highlights of the report for the benefit of the record since the report is not a parliamentary report.
The report recommends the gathering of statistical information that would relate to the ethnicity that is the status of being an aboriginal in the country at the time the native comes in contact with the correctional system. It recommends the generation of some new particularly targeted measuring sticks to determine how well we are

serving the native community in the corrections field. It recommends instituting mechanisms which will address the particular rehabilitative needs of native Canadians.
As an aside, I would like to refer back, as I guess we should, to the justice system of which the corrections system forms a part. We must recall that there are several goals of the justice system taken as a package and the two most important for our discussion here are the deterrence role of the justice system and the rehabilitative goals of the corrections system.
No one wishes to detract from the deterrence function. We have a criminal code in the country that applies to all, including native Canadians, but I think we must admit that there are some environments across the country where our western Judaeo-Christian based criminal code may not be a perfect fit for the native communities. That issue is a conceptual one which is being addressed in other fora.
The second function is a rehabilitative one. I pray that we are not failed to be convinced, in addressing the rehabilitation function of our justice system for native Canadians, that we do not forget that for most native Canadians-not for all, but for most-they live their lives in a society and environment which is other than main street in any of our urban areas.
Therefore, in order to truly and honestly address rehabilitation in the corrections system, we have to do it from where they live their lives. There is a need in our corrections system to institute mechanisms that will dovetail and correspond to the social order in which they find themselves. It is a social order that has been there long before the white man came to this continent.
Another of the recommendations involves the integration of native Canadians into the corrections system's policing systems.
Lastly, it recommends that we have programs at least in a transition period to raise the sensitivity and awareness level of civil servants and volunteers in the area of corrections. Thus, when they work within the system in policing and corrections, whether it be the incarceration phase, a parole phase, a mandatory supervision phase, a residency phase-all of those aspects of corrections-the particular rehabilitative needs of native offenders are
Private Members' Business
responded to in a way that is very sensitive and calculated to produce a result that will serve both the community that that individual lives in and Canadian society as a whole.
My colleagues on this side of the House are supportive of a prompt but comprehensive response of the government to this report. Because it is not a parliamentary report, it does not have a clock running on it. We would be remiss if we did not call the government to task and demand that the report not gather dust and that it respond in a concrete way to the well articulated needs of aboriginal peoples in our corrections system.
