subsubtopic: TASK FORCE ON ABORIGINAL PEOPLES IN FEDERAL CORRECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the motion put by my colleague from Victoria regarding the report on the incarceration of native people of our country.
I listened with care to the comments of my colleague. I must say I was somewhat disappointed in them. First, he said that his comments were not meant to be partisan. If that was non-partisan, I would hate to see him in full flight when he gets partisan with his comments.
This motion is now over a year-and-a-half old. While it is not his fault that it has been on the Order Paper so long, he has been a critic for most of that period of time. He said he was waiting to hear from me as to what recommendations and activity had been going on in this area in the intervening months. A simple call to the department could have helped his curiosity during this period. He would have found that the department has been taking this report very seriously.
What concerns me even more is the fact that he has seen other indications that this minister and his predecessor had taken all of these recommendations seriously. Witness, for example, the example he gave of all of the recommendations regarding the incarceration of women. Part of that involves the incarceration of native women.
As he knows, and he will know, special attention will be given to native women in that particular report. That is what he said, and the very fact that he could recognize that should be clear evidence that we do take this report seriously.

Private Members' Business
The fact is that the report was filed just over 20 months ago. It is one thing to file a report. It is another thing to implement the recommendations, all of which are accepted in principle. The government accepts these recommendations. There then has to be a mechanism for implementing those recommendations. It would be wrong on the part of the government to try to implement them again from Ottawa. I think the hon. member for Victoria would agree to that. What we have to do is implement them in consultation with the people who are most affected by them.
The intervening months have been used, by and large, in consultation with the native community across Canada to make sure that when we do implement these recommendations, it is done in a way that is mindful of the sensitivity of the native community.
In a sense, I suppose I want to compliment the member for bringing this motion forward because it does allow us to put on the record what has been happening in the intervening months. I would like to put on the record the fact that following the completion of the consultations with the provinces, the territories and the national aboriginal organizations, the implementation of the recommendations of the task force was approved in February 1990.
In March 1990 the executive committee of Correctional Service Canada directed the execution of an accelerated implementation plan for the recommendations. I would emphasize the the plan is currently in effect with the objective of implementing the majority of the recommendations within the current fiscal year.
The hon. member opposite happens to be leaving right now just when he finished saying that he wanted on record what was happening. He is already leaving the House.
The 61 recommendations of the task force have been grouped thematically to foster a systematic approach to their application. The categories include recommendations relating to the following areas: institutional programs and operations; the release preparation of aboriginal offenders, post-release programs and support services; personnel matters, including aboriginal cultural awareness training and the recruitment of aboriginal
staff; and the monitoring and evaluation of aboriginal programs and services. In addition, a study of the needs of Inuit offenders was commissioned by Correctional Service Canada to supplement the work of the task force. The study, which was completed in April 1989, produced an additional 29 recommendations which are being put into effect as part of the accelerated implementation plan.
The plan has the following objectives: to increase the number of institutional programs which are relevant to the needs and interests of aboriginal offenders; to increase the full parole release rate for aboriginal offenders to equal at least the rate for non-aboriginal inmates, which is what the member who just left wanted to hear about, to make sure that the aboriginal population would be treated the same way as the non-aboriginal population was treated; to increase the percentage of aboriginal offenders who are successfully serving a portion of their sentences on conditional release; to increase the extent of program delivery for aboriginal persons, and/or agencies; and to implement the development of accurate data collection concerning aboriginal offenders and their program involvement.
The strategies for the implementation of the recommendations of the task force vary in the five regions of Correctional Service Canada. This variation is necessary because each region has a different proportion and distribution of aboriginal offenders. As of September 30, 1990, the distribution was as follows: the Atlantic region had only 31 aboriginal offenders; a small population of aboriginal offenders existed in the Quebec region, which had only 34; the Ontario region had 146; the Prairie region had by far the largest population of aboriginal offenders with 844; and the Pacific region had 246 aboriginal offenders. In total, the number of aboriginal offenders under the responsibility of Correctional Service Canada as of September 30, 1990 was 1,301.
Aboriginal inmates comprise about 11 per cent, not 9 per cent as the member suggested before, but rather it is much worse. It is 11 per cent of the total of approximately 13,000 offenders incarcerated in the federal system. Aboriginal peoples who constitute only 2.5 per cent of the population of Canada are therefore significantly over-represented in the population of federally-incarcerated offenders.
November 27, 1990

In addition, the 194 aboriginal offenders who are serving federal sentences are housed in provincial institutions under the terms of federal-provincial exchange of service agreements. A number of initiatives-and this is what the member wants to hear-toward the provision of equitable decision making and equivalent opportunities for the successful reintegration of aboriginal offenders have been implemented or they have advanced enough to report on. For example, the Atlantic region has established native liaison services in its institutions. Despite the small number of aboriginal inmates in this region the native liaison workers are necessary for the development of culturally sensitive programs and services.
In the Quebec region, the tensions of the past summer between aboriginal people and governments have not slowed down the implementation of initiatives planned in support of the aboriginal and Inuit offenders in that region. For that reason a special program for Inuit offenders is under way at La Macaza Institution. When fully implemented, the program will include academic instruction by a professional person who has experience in teaching Inuit individuals as well as a program of cultural instruction.
There is also significant progress in the Ontario region, and I notice Mr. Speaker, that you want me to hurry along, and in the Prairie region.
The Prairie region has the largest population of incarcerated native persons, with approximately 65 per cent of all federal aboriginal offenders. For that reason, many special initiatives are under way within that region. Let me give some very noteworthy examples, and I will conclude with this, Mr. Speaker: an increase in the number of native liaison workers under contract to a ratio of one worker for every 50 inmates; the solicitation of proposals for the piloting of a new substance abuse treatment program in three institutions; the implementation of three pilot projects for the intensive case preparation of difficult and high-risk cases; the commencement of staffing actions for the placement of community development officers in northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan; the production of printed materials in the Inuit language for placement in four institutions; the modification of regional instructions in order to
Private Members' Business
accommodate the unique dietary needs of Inuit offenders; the establishment of a regional council of aboriginal elders in order to obtain elder input into native issues in the region, this in addition to the native advisory committee of the Prairie region; the implementation of a pilot project on cross-cultural staff training that promotes increased understanding of aboriginal approaches to learning, this in addition to the native awareness training which is already established within the region.
I could go on. There is the Pacific region and so forth. I would hope that the member is satisfied that the government has, is and will continue to take this issue seriously, not simply because it is a government responsibility, but because it is right to do and the aboriginal peoples of our country deserve it.

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE ON ABORIGINAL PEOPLES IN FEDERAL CORRECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I thank my colleague from Victoria for bringing forth this motion so long delayed because of the problems of House business. I think it is nevertheless timely that we discuss this issue, given what has been happening across the country in the last several months.
While I appreciate the statement that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General has brought to the House, in every instance he talks about this has commenced or that has commenced. It has been a year since this motion has been tabled in the House and there should be much more progress, I would say, than has been the case in this situation.
Every time we hear the government answer criticisms as to the delay in implementing programs, we hear that the process of consultation has had to be carried out.
The process of consultation is not that satisfactory either. I am sure that would find some agreement among natives across Canada. This is just another example of the points of contact that native Canadians have had with non-native institutions in this country dating back to time immemorial.
The first institutional contact, of course, was the institution of the reserves and the Indian agent system. When natives were forced on to reserves, they were forced to suffer some of the worst, lowest quality lands that Canada could locate for them.

November 27, 1990
Private Members' Business
They were put on to reserves without adequate funding or the adequate availability of housing, health care, infrastructure and education systems. As a result, those kinds of problems resulted in additional problems which native people were forced to experiences: diseases of poverty, things like tuberculosis and dysentery that killed thousands of our native citizens across this country.
They were oppressed while on the reserves. They had to get permits from the Indian agents in order to leave the reserve. If they violated that permit system, often they were enfranchised and kicked out of their communities. That is the first point of institutional contact that native people made with the non-native society.
The second point of institutional contact, of course, was the residential school system. We have all heard the stories recently about what happened to native children in the residential school system. That system was designed as a systematic approach by the Canadian government and the Department of Indian Affairs to tear native children away from their parents and communities, which were seen as cultural influences, influencing them toward the old native culture, and forcing them into the residential school institutions which were run by the missionary religions.
Those institutional schools totally uprooted children from their communities, something that many of us who have not gone through that school system would find extremely difficult to understand, contemplate or sympathize with because without having gone through that kind of experience, it is veiy difficult to understand.
It is only now that native citizens such as Phil Fontaine who have gone through the experience of the residential school system have begun to tell us about that institutional point of contact with the dominant, non-native society.
In those institutions, native children were terrorized, brutalized, sodomized with the object of destroying their culture, contact with their parents, families and communities, and accepting the culture of the dominant society. That institution was an institution of cultural genocide that achieved its objectives by humiliating and brutalizing those native children.
I do not think any Canadian, having seen that system in operation, could possibly believe that that kind of system could be perpetrated by one Canadian upon another. It is interesting because I am getting to the other institutional points of contact.

Mr. Speaker, if I may speak for a second to the issue of relevance, I think as many native people will tell you today, many of the community and social and individual dysfunctions that have resulted from this particular Canadian institution brought about into Indian communities "for their own good"-to use the term of the Department of Indian Affairs-have resulted in dysfunctions in native communities that result in many natives ending up in another institution, the institution we are talking about now.
I think it is strictly relevant to the discussion that we are having now. If given a few seconds, I will be able to make that relevance clear.
What has happened as a result of the residential school system is that native people have lost their languages, culture, family and community institutions in many cases. That has led to serious individual problems that result in native people coming into contact with the justice system.
For example, when native children came home to their reserves from residential schools, children who had been away for years and years from their parents did not, in many cases, recognize their parents. The understanding of the content of the relationship between parents and their children had been lost. The incest taboo that exists between parents and child had been lost. There are many cases now of domestic sexual abuse and violence that are prevalent on native reserves that many people draw exactly back to this system of the residential school system.
The United Church of Canada has apologized to the native people of Canada for what they have done to the native people through the residential school system. It is regrettable to this day that the Roman Catholic Church has not done that. The Government of Canada, which was the author of the system in the first place, has not seen fit to apologize to native people for what it did to native children, native communities, native parents and to native culture through the residential school system.
November 27, 1990

Those individuals are still paying the price for that institution today. In fact, all Canadians are paying the price for that system today.
The result has been that when natives themselves revolted against the school system and refused to allow them to continue, back in the 1960s, what happened was that native people took control of their own education. They insisted on taking control of their education system, thereby taking it away from the missionaries who had so abused native children and native communities.
What happened is that natives then came into contact with another institutional system of the dominant society. That was the child welfare system. Indian families had been so disintegrated that it gave the white middle-class social service system an opportunity to apprehend those children. Often they were adopted into foster homes or exported to the United States or Europe where they lost their culture altogether. The final point of contact that many native children and many native young people have with this system is the prison system. For this assistant to the Solicitor General to stand up here and say that things are proceeding normally and that things are progressing as quickly as they possible can is a cop-out.
My colleague from Mackenzie recently told me that of the six women in Kingston prison in the last year, three have committed suicide.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today in support of the motion of the member. I am a little surprised at some of the comments I hear when my understanding is that the House is very much in accordance with this motion.

Private Members' Business
In that spirit we want to proceed to speak in favour of the motion because the government certainly takes these questions very seriously. A major factor in our efforts to improve the delivery of correctional services to aboriginal offenders was the task force on federally sentenced women. This was a joint initiative between the public and volunteer sectors.
The task force was made up of two committees, a steering committee and a working group, which were co-chaired by representatives of the Correctional Service Canada and the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies. As my colleague probably knows, the membership of the task force included federally sentenced women, community, aboriginal women's groups, and a variety of governmental agency representatives as well. The task force released its report in April 1990. As I have said, that has had a major impact on the thinking of this government.
There are approximately 260 federally sentenced women incarcerated in various places in Canada. The total number of women offenders is generally a stable number, as my colleague is aware, representing about 2 per cent of the total federal offender population. Of this group, about 15 per cent are aboriginal women. Specifically, according to the latest statistics available to me, native women in prison number about 46.
Approximately 200 of women at any given time are under the control of the federal government are under the Community Release Supervision Program. About 50 per cent of all federally sentenced women are accommodated at the only federal prison for women, which is a multi-level institution located in Kingston. Most of the remaining women are serving their sentences in provincial institutions due to a federal-provincial exchange of service agreements.
Additionally, since March 1990, 11 women who are serving federal sentences and who have earned the privilege of a minimum security rating have been housed in a new minimum security institution which is also located in Kingston.
Due in part to their small numbers, there are several long-standing and unresolved issues which have placed women at a disadvantage in the federal facility for women at Kingston. Many of the women, for example, are very far from their families, their cultures, and their communities. Like their male counterparts, many aboriginal women offenders come from the prairie provinces. They already face cultural isolation. In addition, when they are removed geographically from their communities they face additional isolation. As well most of the inmates are whites, so there is a cultural separation that creates many problems.
Because it was originally designed as a maximum security institution, the prison for women must accommodate a whole variety of security classification levels. This results in the overclassification of many women. That reduces their opportunities to access other community facilities and programs that are geared and suited to their individual security needs. While the minimum security facility for women helps to address some of these problems, especially, for example, the problem of geographical dislocation, like the prison for women it too is in Kingston. It can only accommodate 11 minimum security women, which means there is a great and crying need.
There is also a lack of programs and services to respond to the unique needs of women. The task force found that physical and sexual abuse is part of the history of many federally sentenced women and that the incidence of such abuse is particularly high among aboriginal women.
In fact, 90 per cent of aboriginal women offenders told the task force members that they had been physically abused during their lifetimes. Usually this abuse had taken place over long periods of time. This compared to 61 per cent of non-aboriginal women. In addition, the number of aboriginal women who talked of being sexually abused was as high as 61 per cent as compared to 50 per cent of non-aboriginal population. Many of these women expressed a desire for individual counselling to deal with these experiences.
There are very few services available in provincial institutions for survivors of physical and/or sexual abuse, a fact which disadvantages many of the federally sentenced women who reside in these facilities through the exchange of service agreements with the provinces, as I mentioned before. Furthermore, aboriginal women really look to having some culturally appropriate programs- they need these-which will help them to recover from their experience with either kind of abuse.
There are other program inequities which result from the placement of federally sentenced women in provincial institutions. These facilities, for example, are not
November 27, 1990

geared to the needs of longer term offenders, people who will be in the population for a longer period of time. They do not offer programs that will contribute to the eventual reintegration of these women into the community. There is very little effective pre-release planning or programming to help these women.
Furthermore, it is somewhat demoralizing for women who are facing long-term incarceration to be housed in provincial institutions with other offenders who are there for only a short period of time. Because of the time differences friendships are broken up just when they are beginning. This creates much greater pressures for the women who are there as federal offenders. The facilities are continually releasing women who are there with shorter sentences, reducing the opportunities for friendship.
In its report the task force presented a number of recommendations including the following. It suggested that we close the prison for women and the establishment of four federally operated regional facilities for women serving federal sentences. Additionally it suggested the creation of an aboriginal healing lodge, which would serve as an incarceration option for aboriginal women who are under sentence.
The aboriginal healing lodge would be designed in consultation with aboriginal people. It will operate from a unique cultural perspective, which would put a high value on spiritual leadership, as well on things that are culturally appropriate in terms of role modelling. The services will be provided by professionals who have had some experience with the native traditions and cultures. In addition, the healing lodge will respond to the concerns expressed by many aboriginal women offenders that they are not dealing with people who understand their culture and have experiences relevant to their particular needs and that they are not comfortable talking with non-aboriginal people about sexual or other kinds of abuse.
The lodge will provide the following to aboriginal offenders: a safe place for women of aboriginal descent; a caring attitude toward self, family and community; a belief in individualized client specific planning so that people are treated like people rather than like numbers; an understanding of the healing role of children who, in
Private Members' Business
aboriginal cultures, are considered to be closer to the spirit world; and pride in surviving difficult backgrounds and personal experiences.
The lodge will also respond to the concerns of aboriginal women around issues of racism. Aboriginal programs should reflect the cultures and spiritual experiences of federally sentenced women who feel that they have suffered from marginalization and from erosion of then-culture in mainstream Canadian society.
On September 26, the Solicitor General announced the government's response to the recommendations of the task force on federally sentenced women. Canadians can be very proud that the response included full support for the major recommendations of the task force.
The government has made a commitment to ensure that new regional correctional facilities for women will be constructed within four years. In the meantime, Correctional Service Canada is committed to implementing the short-term recommendations which were also submitted by the task force and which aimed at improving conditions in the prison for women.
The recommendations calling for the elimination of transfers from provincial correctional institutions for women will be implemented. The recommendation calling for the daily presence of an aboriginal elder at the prison for women to minister to the spiritual needs has been partially implemented. The service is also in the process of implementing such measures as funded visits with family and enhanced telephone contacts at no additional cost to the inmate.
This will be of particular value and of great assistance to aboriginal women because, as I pointed out, most of them suffer from serious geographical dislocation from their families, their communities, and their cultures.
Finally, the recommendation which calls for the provision of a national aboriginal liaison worker has been successfully implemented already. This worker facilitates information sharing and assists aboriginal women in maintaining contact with their families, cultures, and communities cross Canada.
Once again, we would like to support the motion of the hon. member opposite and say that we whole-heartedly support all and any measures that can make the

Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased for this opportunity to comment on the motion and to offer my support to it in principle. I share the desire of the hon. member for Victoria, as do most if not all members on both sides of this House, to implement any changes that are going to make Correction Service Canada more effective and able to improve rehabilitative services to all inmates of both sexes and all races.
The issue raised in this motion is serious. Although it is obvious that I am going to be more supportive of actions that have been taken since the task force recommendations than was the hon. member for Victoria, we are both going to agree that there is still need for more.
I also edited my comments very carefully so that they fit into the allotted time. I notice that the time has been reduced somewhat, so I would like to offer my conclusion and then give my argument because I do not want to leave out the conclusion.
My conclusion is that I feel there has been a significant evolution in aboriginal offences services over the last two decades, but there are still facts that are outstanding and troubling. They include the fact that fewer aboriginal offenders have been granted full parole by the National Parole Board. Second, when aboriginal offenders were granted some form of conditional release, it occurred later in their sentence than in the case of non-native offenders. Third, aboriginal offenders were more likely to have their parole revoked than non-native offenders.
These are serious concerns, but I believe that the federal government, through the intervention of Correctional Service Canada, has, is, and will continue to take every possible step in implementing the recommendations of the task force on aboriginal peoples in federal institutions.
I said that I support the motion in principle. I would suggest that so does the federal government and Correctional Service Canada. The federal government and the CSC have already taken measures to implement the majority of the recommendations within this current fiscal year. I say "the majority of the recommendations" because some of them, those which relate to affirmative
action, to personnel recruitment and development, and to the statistical adaptation of psychometric diagnostic tests for use with aboriginal people, as well as some which require other agency participation, will require a phased in implementation that will extend beyond the current fiscal year.
The hon. member for Victoria has spent time, as have I, on the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General. Among other things, we have read and reviewed the mission statement Correctional Service Canada. For those who have not heard or read it, I would like to add it to the record of this debate.
Correctional Service Canada, as part of the criminal justice system, contributes to the protection of society by actively encouraging and assisting offenders to become law-abiding citizens, while exercising reasonable, safe, secure and humane control. Through this mission statement, Correctional Service Canada recognizes its responsibility toward all offenders, including aboriginals. Further, it recognizes what it calls core value number 2, that "the offender has the potential to live as a law-abiding citizen".
The mission statement also articulates a specific strategy objective in relation to core value number 2, which is "to ensure that the needs of female and aboriginal offenders are properly addressed".
Many other objectives which are reflected in the CSC strategic plan for the period of 1990-91 to 1992-93 are also of special importance in order to meet the needs of aboriginal offenders. They are all relevant to the question before us, so again I am quoting:
1.2	to ensure that policies and procedures affecting offenders are communicated in such a way that they can be understood by offenders and are readily accessible to them;
2.3	to provide programs to assist offenders in meeting their individual needs, in order to enhance their potential for reintegration as law-abiding citizens;
2.4	to ensure that offenders are productively occupied and have access to a variety of work and educational opportunities to meet their needs for growth and personal development;
2.6	to ensure that program needs are considered when making placement and transfer decisions;

3.8	to provide staff training and development opportunities that are based on the achievement of our Mission, develop the full potential of staff members, and emphasize interpersonal skills, leadership, and respect for the unique differences and needs of all offenders.
Corporate objective number II of the plan is:
To develop and implement policies and programs to address the specific needs and reduce the potential recidivism of federally sentenced women, native offenders, violent offenders, sex offenders, mentally disordered offenders and inmates serving long sentence.
The innovative projects and enhanced services for aboriginal offenders are aimed directly at these strategic and corporate objectives.
These objectives do not answer all of the recommendations contained in the report of April 1989, but it is important for this House and everyone concerned about the recommendations and their impact on Correctional Service Canada to know that they exist. They are stated objectives of Correctional Service Canada written for this year which illustrate that the recommendations of the committee are being acted upon and that the programs are being influenced.
As I mentioned earlier, the federal government and Correctional Service of Canada have already taken measures through a national accelerated implementation plan to implement the majority of these recommendations within the current fiscal year. The plan has the following five objectives:
to increase institutional programs that are relevant for Aboriginal offenders, and to assist in their preparation for success on conditional release;
to increase the release rate on full parole for Aboriginal offenders;
to increase the percentage of Aboriginal offenders who are successfully serving a portion of their sentence on conditional release;
to increase program delivery by Aboriginal persons and/or agencies; and
to develop accurate data collection concerning Aboriginal offenders and their program involvement.

Since my election and appointment to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General, I have had the opportunity to look at corrections in a different and hopefully

Mr. Speaker, as you know, I am expressing some concern about a response that was given to a question I asked almost at the time that the member for Victoria submitted his motion.
I asked at that time the Minister of Justice, having received the 1989 report of the Human Rights Commissioner of Canada, if she would act on a recommendation proposed by the Human Rights Commissioner for a Royal commission of the stature of the Bilingualism and Biculturalism commission into the issue of the relationship between natives and non-natives in Canada. At that time the minister responded: "It is not up to me to institute a Royal commission. It should be a decision of the Prime Minister and his government".
As Mr. Speaker will recall, in his 1988 report, the Human Rights Commissioner pointed to the situation of native people in Canada. He indicated that the grand promise of equal opportunity that forms the central purpose of Canadian human rights stands in stark contrast with the conditions in which many native people of Canada lived. He pointed out that the treatment of native Canadians is a national shame. He called upon the people of Canada to set up a Royal commission which would inquire into the relationship between Canada and its native citizens, a Royal commission that would have the stature of the Bilingualism and Biculturalism commission that set the language and cultural debate between the two nations of Canada's dominant society.
At the time of his annual report of 1989 the Human Rights Commissioner came back to the House of Commons recognizing that little if anything had happened to correct the situation or improve the situation of native people in Canada. He talked about the conditions under which native people in this country lived. He said to the people of Canada: "Anyone who thinks the game has been won need only to glance at the statistics or have a
closer look at the shattering truth that lies behind them. Some of the social indicators may have improved, but the condition of aboriginal life is still a long way from matching the expectations of Canadian society as a whole".
He also said: "Make no mistake about it, these are human rights problems. If there is any single issue on which Canada cannot hold its head high in the international community, any single area in which we can be accused of falling down on our obligations, it is in this area of aboriginal relations". Again he called upon the people of Canada, the Parliament of Canada, and the Government of Canada. He said: "It is for this reason we have suggested that a thorough going inquiry into these problems modelled on the Royal commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism of 25 years ago might play a useful role in achieving consensus without being used as an excuse for delaying important developments".
Again the chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission called on Parliament and called on government to take action to establish a Royal commission into the relations between Canada's native people and its dominant society.
Just a few days ago, on September 21, in an act almost of desperation and frustration coming out of the Oka crisis this summer, again Human Rights Commissioner Max Yalden made public a report to Parliament in which he again called on the Canadian government, saying: "Progress has been too slow and little if anything has been done." He called upon the Canadian government to establish a Royal commission into the relations among Canada's aboriginal people, the government, and the people of Canada. Again nothing was done.
I am concerned that as a result of what is happening with the recommendations of the Royal commission, native people are becoming more and more frustrated and perceive more and more that Canada does not attach any priority to their problems. In fact, they see the Prime Minister playing games with the issue of a Royal commission. At one time, he holds it out as a carrot to the Manitoba chiefs in order to try to get the chiefs to silence Elijah Harper when he is standing up in the legislature and saying no to the Meech Lake Accord. Another time he is holding it as a stick to the natives. When Meech Lake died he said: "You are responsible
November 27, 1990

and, as a result, you are not going to get a Royal commission."
When he talked to the First Nations Congress in British Columbia about the possibility of either having a process to set up land claims negotiations in that province or having a Royal commission, the native people in British Columbia said that they wanted both but that they did not want the selection of one to jeopardize the other.
More recently we have heard Lowell Murray say: "No, this Royal commission will not be struck until the Spicer committee reports on July 1."
It is time to end this process of manipulation. It is time for the government to call a Royal commission. It is evident that the problems out there need the examination of a Royal commission. The aboriginal people want it. The people of Canada want it. When is the government going to follow the people of Canada and do the bidding of the people of Canada?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issues raised by the Canadian Human Rights Commission are serious ones of concern to the federal government.
As the hon. member noted, the report recommends a Royal commission, one modelled on the Bilingual and Biculturalism Royal commission of 25 years ago.
The Prime Minister told this House of Commons on September 25, 1990 that the government had been discussing an agenda with native leaders to address issues of concern to Canada's native people. The Prime Minister outlined this government's plans to preserve the special place of first nations in this country, based on the aboriginal and treaty rights recognized in the Constitution.
The agenda will have four main pillars: the land claims, the economic and social conditions on reserves, the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments, and the concerns of aboriginal peoples in contemporary life. Fundamental to the agenda are changes to the Indian Act, with the objective of enlarging the aboriginal capacity for self-government within the framework of the Canadian Constitution.
Adjournment Debate
However, at the present time many of the departments of this government are already at work on the issues that have been identified by the Human Rights Commission. The Ministry of the Solicitor General, the Ministry of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and the Department of Justice are among those departments that are addressing separately and jointly the question of aboriginal rights, native justice, self-government, and other pressing issues of concern to the people of Canada, aboriginal and non-aboriginal alike.
Since 1977 the Department of Justice has funded the Native Court Worker Program in conjunction with the provinces and territories. The purpose of this program is to assist natives who become involved in the criminal justice system and to enhance the awareness of those involved in the criminal justice system concerning the values, customs, and socio-economic conditions of native people.
In most cases the program is delivered by a native agency which varies from province to province. In British Columbia, for example, the carrier agency is the Native Court Worker and Counselling Association, while in Ontario the Friendship Centres deliver the program.
In June 1990 the Minister of Justice, meeting with her provincial and territorial colleagues, agreed to sponsor a national conference on aboriginal justice jointly. Fifty per cent of those participants will be aboriginal people. The conference will be co-sponsored by the Yukon whose Minister of Justice originally proposed the gathering.
The Marshall inquiry made a number of recommendations concerning the criminal justice system and aboriginal people in Nova Scotia, and since the report was released representatives of our government have been available to work with provincial and Micmac representatives to act upon these recommendations.
I think the hon. member would, and should, agree that the federal government has demonstrated by these and other initiatives that it is deeply committed to addressing the problems faced by aboriginal people in this country today, and we have every intention of continuing to do so.

Adjournment Debate GOODS AND SERVICES TAX

Mr. Speaker, I have raised a number of questions regarding the GST and the way it affects lower-income Canadians.
Over the past several months, we have heard the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare state repeatedly that families with incomes of $30,000 or less will, in fact, be better off under the goods and services tax than they are now. This statement is open to challenge on a number of grounds. In fact, the GST will not help middle and lower-income families in any way, shape or form. That is why, of course, 80 per cent or so of Canadians want the tax scrapped and want a fair taxation system in the country.
While arguing the benefits of the GST for lower-income Canadians, the government often refers to the GST tax credit as the measure that takes the burden of the GST off this group. This, of course, is simply not the case. The tax credit is only partially indexed to inflation, first of all, meaning that its real value will decline each year and that the income threshold for receiving the credit will also decline. As the years go by, fewer and fewer families will be eligible for the credit and those who are eligible will receive less money.
If the government was serious about using the GST tax credit to assist the less well off, it would have indexed it fully to inflation. By not doing so, the government is making it clear to lower-income Canadians that they will bear a greater tax burden in the years ahead. Lower-income Canadians will be paying more tax and receiving less in the form of the GST tax credit in the future.
Another problem with the tax credits under the GST is that by earning less, a person does not necessarily receive a higher credit. In other words, those who are less well off will not necessarily be compensated any more. For instance, a single person earning $6,000 is eligible for a tax credit of $190. A single person earning between $14,000 and $24,000 is eligible for a tax credit of $280. Whatever the case, it is clear that this will not compensate those Canadians for the increased costs due to the GST.
Presumably, the rationale for giving those with lower incomes a lower GST credit is that they will, in fact,
spend less of their money on GST taxable items. But they will spend a higher proportion of their income on taxable goods and services. The lower a person's income, the larger the proportion they will spend on essential goods and services.
Lower-income earners do not have the luxury of putting some money aside in tax-free savings account such as RRSPs. Canadians living below the poverty line are not going to be savers. In fact, with this government's regressive policies, such as cutbacks to family allowances, cuts to transfer payments to the provinces for health and post-secondary education, cap on CAP for British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario, and the privatization and reduction in benefits for the Unemployment Insurance Plan, few ordinary Canadians will be saving at all.
Yet another call for concern about the efficacy of the GST tax credit is that a number of provinces have indicated that they may consider the credit as income and thus reclaim the credit from welfare recipients. In other words, many welfare recipients, the poorest of the poor, will have absolutely no protection from this regressive GST at all.
The Minister of Finance, and others, have indicated in the House and elsewhere that they would strongly encourage the provinces not to take this step of robbing the poor of their GST tax credit. But, the government has not made a firm and absolute commitment to ensuring that this will not occur. It must make such a commitment immediately to stop its ideological cousins and provincial Conservative governments from grabbing this meagre GST tax credit from the poorest of Canadians.
This, Mr. Speaker, is particularly a problem in Alberta and my province of Saskatchewan, which has not yet indicated that it has no intention of taking the GST credit from social assistance recipients, and indeed appears to be considering the matter very strongly.
In addition to this, there are many other claims about the miracle of the GST. The Minister of Finance has told us that many products will actually cost less under the GST. He has given examples such as washing machines, driers, and new automobiles. These items are generally not in the budget of lower income families. Lower-income families, if they can afford a car at all, will buy used cars which are newly taxed under the goods and services
November 27, 1990

tax. It is hard to visualize just how lower-income families will benefit under the goods and services tax.
In addition, the minister's statements assuring us that some items will cost less under the goods and services tax because of the removal of the manufacturers' sales tax are based on the assumption that manufacturers will pass this saving on to the consumer. Yet we have heard on numerous occasions from manufacturers saying that they have no intention of passing on the savings. Instead, we will see many items simply jump 7 per cent in price beginning January 1, 1991, if indeed the tax is implemented.
What about the timing of the implementation of the GST. Canada is presently in a recession and governments across the country are running deficit budgets and, at the same time, trying to reduce the deficits. The way in which they are trying to do this will inevitably lead us down the road to cuts in social assistance, health services, post-secondary education programs and so on. These are the sorts of cuts we have seen from this Conservative government and provincial Conservative governments.
During a recession, a time when low-income Canadians need social safety nets the most, it appears that they will be reduced, both at the federal and provincial level.
The government has acknowledged but under-estimated greatly the inflationary effect of the GST. While this will make it more difficult for all Canadians to make ends meet, once again lower-income Canadians will be the hardest hit. Lower-income Canadians, if employed at all, are most likely to be employed in non-unionized, part-time and temporary jobs. They have no bargaining power with their employer, or with the government, to index their wages or, if they are on social assistance, no bargaining power to indexed or social assistance cheques to inflation. The latest example of this is the partially-indexed GST credit, a small compensation to the poor for the great hardship the GST will bring them. They will fall further and further behind in times of inflation.
In closing, Canadians have asked for tax reform but they have not asked for the GST. The GST is clearly not what they have in mind. When they want a tax reform, they want a fair taxation system where those who can afford to pay more do so. The more affluent, who are
Adjournment Debate
now the subject of tax loopholes, should be paying their fair share. The 118,700 profitable corporations which paid no tax last year should also be paying their fair share. The GST is regressive and hurts lower-income Canadians the most. It is not fair that a welfare mother earning $6,000 a year pays the same 7 per cent tax that a corporate executive earning $200,000 a year pays.
In closing, it is time the government listened to the concerns of Canadian families by helping them, instead of punishing them for being less well off. Surely not being able to see their own children eat properly-we all know that one in four children in Saskatchewan goes hungry-is punishment enough. It is time that the government decided to implement a fair tax system and scrap the goods and services tax.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the assertions of the hon. member for Saskatoon- Clark's Crossing, this government has had a great interest in fair taxation.
We have worked to eliminate the special treatment that is used to permit those of greater means to pay less tax. Consequently, higher-income Canadians and profitable corporations now pay taxes which are more commensurate with their earnings.
First, we converted personal exemptions and many deductions to tax credits to improve fairness, and reduced or eliminated many special tax breaks. We also eliminated or reduced many special corporate tax breaks, and broadened the tax base so that profitable corporations pay tax.
In the 1989 budget, the government announced a new large corporations tax for Canadian corporate capital in excess of $10 million. Effectively January 1, 1991, the large corporations tax will be raised and that rate will be a 15 per cent increase. This tax will help ensure that big business pays its fair share of tax.
The proposed goods and services tax is designed to further improve the fairness of taxation in Canada. Under the GST, the distribution of the tax burden will be more progressive.
Wealthy Canadians will pay their fair share. They will not be able to avoid the GST. They tend to consume more and, therefore, will pay more on average on the

November 27, 1990
Adjournment Debate
sales tax. With the GST credit, families with incomes of up to $30,000 a year will have more after-tax income than they do now. This includes three-quarters of families headed by seniors or single parent families. In total, some 8.7 million families and individuals will receive credit cheques.
As well, basic groceries and residential rents will be exempt under the GST, further reducing the tax burden of lower income Canadians.
Before the government introduced refundable sales tax credits in 1986, low income Canadians paid much more federal sales tax as a percentage of their income than the higher income brackets. Since 1986, the federal sales tax credit has been increased three times. With the introduction of the GST, the refundable sales tax credit will be enhanced once more, the monetary value of the credit will be increased and the income eligibility threshold to receive the credit will be raised. As a result, lower income earners will pay much less as a percentage of their income than those in higher income brackets.
The hon. member is also of the opinion that business will fail to pass on to the consumer the savings of the existing sales tax replaced by the GST.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with regard to a question that I posed on November 20 this year to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology.
On that particular occasion I asked the minister if he would reconsider the decision that he had made to kill the Synfuels project, which affects the people of eastern Nova Scotia.
This particular project had widespread support across the province. In fact, April 18, 1990, was the first time in a long time the Nova Scotia House of Assembly passed an all-party resolution. Even the socialists and the Conservatives supported the Liberal Party in Nova Scotia in supporting the Synfuels project, which in its very essence is where coal and crude oil come together to form a particular product, thereafter being exported to various countries and to various businesses in order to produce energy.
Unfortunately, the Government of Canada has killed this particular project. If there is any further testimony, as codified in the Chronicle Herald of November 16,1990, it said: "Ottawa kills Synfuels Project".
There are three major advantages of this particular project. I would have hoped that the minister in his wisdom, and particularly the officials of the department, would have seen fit to sit down with the principals of the Synfuels project to debate and discuss with them a plan of action in order to see this particular project realized.
I should note for the edification of members in this House that we in Atlantic Canada, partly because of our geography, and also because of our limited sources of energy at the present time, are dependent to a large extent on the importation of foreign oil, so much so that it has caused provincial governments down through the years, going back to the mid 1950s, and perhaps even before that, to come up with an energy policy which is supportive of the resources which we have in the boundaries within our provinces and to utilize that not only to create jobs, but also to have a stable supply, if you will, of energy for the taxpayers of that province.
With coal being used on the Synfuels project and the technology that is readily available, one could get approximately five barrels of oil per tonne of coal. That is an amazing sum, Mr. Speaker, in view of the large quantities of imported oil that we have in the province of Nova Scotia.
There is a clear advantage for Canadians from coast to coast, but particularly for those of us in Atlantic Canada, namely, that there would be less of a dependence on foreign oil. I do not have to point out to the parliamentary secretary who will be responding to my assertions here today the need for stable supplies of energy across this

great country of ours. We just have to look to the Persian Gulf where the stability of oil supplies which feed many parts of the world are certainly in question. Of course, the consequential effect that that has with regard to rising energy prices is a concern for all Canadians.
The environmental advantages of this particular project are well documented and well supported by environmentalists and those of us who are concerned with good public policy for Canadians in that area of our country.
Cape Breton has coal which is low in ash, but it is very high in sulphur. It is a very soft coal and it would be utilized very easily with regard to new coal technologies and the processes that go into place in terms of changing that particular coal into a liquid substance, which is thereafter used in energy and used for domestic purposes. There is a real environmental advantage.
There is a regional development advantage. As I said on November 20, as my colleagues have said on previous occasions, and of course as I have said this repeatedly in the House, the construction phase of this project would result in approximately 500 construction jobs. It would provide direct and indirect jobs of approximately 2,000. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, in terms of an economic bonanza, if you will, in that area of eastern Nova Scotia, it would be very helpful.
I want to point out to the parliamentary secretary that in that area of the province unemployment is exceedingly high. In fact, the figures from the Department of Employment and Immigration base it at approximately 17.3 per cent. For those of us who have the privilege, and I say it is a privilege to live in that area of this country, we know it to be much worse than 17 per cent. In fact, municipal leaders in many parts of my constituency, namely Glace Bay, would indicate that it is much higher than 17 per cent and at 30 and 40 per cent.
Hibernia will cost $5.2 billion of taxpayers money. The Lloydminster project will cost taxpayers $1.2 billion. The OSLO project will cost Canadian taxpayers $4.1 billion. All those compared to the Synfuels Project, with benefits in terms of environment, regional development, jobs indirect and direct, as well as the construction, and of
Adjournment Debate
course the benefits in terms of less dependence on foreign oil, which will cost a mere $400 million.
In closing, I am the first to admit that this is indeed a lot of money. Therefore, it underlines the need for the the Government of Canada to sit down with principals of the Synfuels Project and work out a plan which is equitable for the principals and for the Government of Canada, but more importantly beneficial to Canadians who happen to live in the Atlantic region and reside in the eastern part of Nova Scotia.
I invite the very able parliamentary secretary to stand in his place and give us the kind of reassurance that taxpayers in that area of the country so rightly deserve.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to respond to the question raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton-Richmond East concerning the Scotia Synfuels project.
The project, in a variety of configurations, has been examined and analysed by federal representatives for nearly ten years. During the initial years of its development, the project enjoyed financial and technical support provided by a consortium, directed by private sector interests with the necessary expertise to carry out the project. Over time, the members of this consortium abandoned the project for technical or financial reasons.
During that time, the federal government invested approximately $2 million, together with the private sector, in testing procedures and project-related technology studies. We wanted to work with the project sponsors to find out whether we could develop viable markets and thus use the human and natural resources of Cape Breton.
Tests indicated that the technology could be used but additional detailed engineering studies were necessary to ensure that the proposed facility would produce the forecast quantity and quality of synthetic fuel. Federal and provincial representatives met with the project leaders on many occasions over the years in order to make the project a success. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, we co-operated very closely and we invested taxpayers' money. Briefly, we did our share to make the project materialize.

Adjournment Debate
During discussions with the sponsor last year, it was frequently pointed out that a project of this size could not proceed without a qualified and dynamic principal partner from the private sector. This essential ingredient could not be found, Mr. Speaker, which means that all the risks would have to be taken by Canadian taxpayers. In addition to the requested investment tax credits totalling $200 million, the project would require hundreds of millions of dollars in additional financial assistance, in the form of interest reductions and credit insurance.
As I pointed out, the project sponsors have had every opportunity to develop the project and meet the appropriate people to make the project a success. At the present time, after years of activity, the project has not yet been finalized. Funds that were supposed to come from the private sector are not there and have not even been identified. Briefly, it is no use having further meetings on the subject, Mr. Speaker, unless there is a significant change with respect to private sector interests.
